operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.
workflow: Audit statutory fee caps, claim windows, and chain-of-title encumbrances
Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts
metrics: Gross spread / contingent fee per case

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory fee-cap compression or administrative hold
platform_risks.trigger: Jurisdiction updates finder fee limits, waiting periods, or filing documentation rules
platform_risks.impact: Reduced net fee margin or extended cash conversion cycle
platform_risks.detection_metric: County/state rejection notice rate and days-to-payout variance
platform_risks.fallback: Diversify across multi-state dockets and use attorney-backed filing partnerships where required

operator_plays.name: SAM.gov / Municipal RFP Scraping & Prime-Subcontractor Spread Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Scrape federal SAM.gov, state procurement portals, and municipal bid boards for low-bid-density service solicitations (janitorial, grounds, courier, translation, IT staffing), pairing compliant proposal automation with vetted local fulfillment subcontractors for a 15–30% management spread.
inputs: SAM.gov Contract Opportunities API & state/municipal e-procurement feeds
Historical FPDS award pricing benchmark database
Vetted local subcontractor network with FAR limitation-on-subcontracting compliance
workflow: Screen daily federal, state, and municipal RFPs/RFQs with <3 historical bidders and clear unit-price schedules
Benchmark winning historical unit rates via FPDS/FOIA award records and lock in binding back-to-back quotes from insured local operators
Submit compliant bid packages and manage billing, insurance, and QA reporting while retaining a 15–30% prime-management or authorized broker spread
metrics: Bid-to-award win rate (%) on low-competition solicitations

platform_risks.failure_mode: FAR 52.219-14 (Limitations on Subcontracting) violation or illegal pass-through scheme
platform_risks.trigger: Bidding small-business set-aside contracts and subcontracting 100% of the work to non-similarly-situated entities without performing required prime share
platform_risks.impact: Contract termination for default, False Claims Act liability, or SAM.gov debarment
platform_risks.detection_metric: Subcontracted labor-cost percentage strictly within FAR 52.219-14 limits (<=50% for services unless partnering with similarly situated small businesses)
platform_risks.fallback: Bid unrestricted commercial/municipal contracts without set-aside caps, or team exclusively with 'similarly situated entities' under 13 CFR § 125.6

operator_plays.name: Multi-Account Presale Code & Limited-Mintage Allocation Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Operating hundreds of aged, human-scored 'free' fan-club, ticketing (Ticketmaster Verified Fan / AXS), U.S. Mint, and limited-edition luxury/collectible accounts—each backed by unique residential proxies, aged browser profiles, and virtual card numbers (VCCs)—to multiply lottery/queue odds by 100x–500x on strict 'limit 1–4 per account' releases trading at instant 50–300% secondary-market premiums.
inputs: Aged ticketing, fan-club, and sovereign-mint account fleet with clean purchase histories
Anti-detect browser matrix with residential ISP proxies and unique SIM/SMS verification lines
Corporate virtual credit card (VCC) issuance API (Extend/Ramp/Slash) with distinct billing descriptors
workflow: Monitor upcoming concert tours, playoff games, U.S. Mint numismatic releases, and limited collectible drops with secondary-market spreads >=50%
Register the aged account fleet across presale lotteries and waiting rooms to secure high-priority access codes and low queue positions
Execute checkouts strictly on high-margin allocations (front-row/pit seats, low-mintage proof coins) using isolated VCCs per household profile
Flip allocations immediately via direct consignment, verified ticket exchanges (StubHub/SeatGeek/Vivid API), or pre-committed wholesale buyers
metrics: Presale code / top-1,000 queue-position hit rate (%) across the account cluster
Net realized secondary-market spread (%) after exchange/consignment fees
Inventory hold time (hours/days from checkout to settled resale payout)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Order cancellation or queue-score penalty from device/payment fingerprint linkage
platform_risks.trigger: Reusing identical billing addresses, card BINs, or browser WebGL/Canvas fingerprints across Household-Limit-restricted drops
platform_risks.impact: Canceled orders, revoked presale codes, or permanent account flagging
platform_risks.detection_metric: Post-checkout order survival rate (%) and queue-score tier telemetry
platform_risks.fallback: Maintain genuine distributed buyer consortiums with unique residential addresses, distinct bank BINs, and pre-sold wholesale buyer commitments before checkout

operator_plays.name: Section 321 "De Minimis" & Border Bonded-Warehouse Tariff Split-Shipping Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Routing bulk sea/air container imports for high-tariff DTC and marketplace brands into Tijuana (IMMEX) or Canadian border-zone bonded 3PL warehouses instead of US ports, then fulfilling individual US consumer orders across the border daily under 19 U.S.C. § 1321 (Section 321 Entry Type 86)—legally eliminating 15%–42.5% customs duties on qualifying consumer parcels and charging brands 35–50% of the saved tariff bill plus 3PL fulfillment fees.
inputs: USITC Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) database cross-referenced against US Customs Bill-of-Lading import records (ImportYeti / Panjiva / Datamyne)
Nearshore Mexican IMMEX or Canadian customs-bonded fulfillment center 5–15 miles from San Ysidro/Otay Mesa or Windsor/Blaine border crossings
Automated CBP ACE Entry Type 86 manifest software transmitting 10-digit HTS and consignee data per individual consumer parcel
workflow: Scrape public maritime Bill-of-Lading records to identify US apparel, footwear, luggage, and consumer-goods brands importing 20+ containers/yr in 18%–37.5% HTS duty brackets
Divert the client's ocean containers in-bond (IT/T&E bond) directly to the nearshore border-zone fulfillment facility without paying US bulk entry duties
Sync the warehouse WMS with the brand's Shopify/Amazon store so each US consumer order (<$800 retail value, 1 per person per day) is picked, packed, and cleared via CBP Entry Type 86 at $0 duty
Line-item bill the brand for standard pick-and-pack fulfillment plus a 35–50% contingency split of the verified customs duties eliminated
metrics: Annualized customs duty eliminated ($500k–$10M+/yr per enterprise brand client)
Net tariff-savings share + 3PL margin ($) per parcel cleared across the border
CBP Type 86 automated release rate (>99.4%) and border transit time (<6 hours to USPS/FedEx domestic injection)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory exclusion of specific Section 301 country-of-origin SKUs from Section 321 de minimis eligibility
platform_risks.trigger: Executive/statutory rulemaking removing China-origin Section 301 HTS codes from Entry Type 86 eligibility or tightening 10-digit HTS description rules
platform_risks.impact: Loss of Section 321 duty exemption on affected country-of-origin SKUs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Real-time HTS + Country-of-Origin eligibility screen in the WMS before container booking
platform_risks.fallback: Focus on non-301 origin goods (Vietnam, India, EU, Bangladesh, Cambodia) where high MFN duties (16%–32% on apparel/footwear/textiles) remain 100% Section 321 exempt, and pair with CBP First-Sale Valuation for remaining SKUs

operator_plays.name: Authorized-Distributor "Diversion" & Grey-Market Luxury / Medical Consumables Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Exploiting multinational manufacturers' 35–60% regional price discrimination by using foreign corporate purchasing entities to buy container-loads of 100% authentic branded goods (luxury fragrances, prestige cosmetics, Swiss watches, OTC diabetic test strips, salon haircare, OEM imaging supplies) from over-quota authorized distributors in emerging/EMEA/LATAM markets and importing them into US off-price retail (TJX, Costco, Burlington) and Amazon wholesale channels under the Supreme Court's First-Sale Doctrine (*Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons*).
inputs: Global wholesale price-book matrix comparing US net distributor pricing against EMEA, LATAM, Eastern European, and Asian-Pacific tier-1 distributor net pricing
Foreign purchasing subsidiaries (UAE, Poland, Panama, Singapore, Cyprus) with clean trade references and escrow inspection facilities
SGS/Bureau Veritas pre-shipment authenticity verification and batch-code sanitization SOPs
workflow: Identify authentic global SKUs with >40% wholesale price spreads between emerging-market distributor books and US off-price wholesale demand
Approach regional authorized distributors near end-of-quarter who need to move $500k–$5M in excess allocation to hit their manufacturer volume-tier rebate
Purchase the sealed master cases via a foreign trading entity, conduct third-party SGS lot authentication, and remove secondary distributor tracking labels that could identify the source distributor
Import the goods legally under First-Sale exhaustion and flip on back-to-back POs to US off-price retail chains, pharmacy wholesalers, and verified marketplace aggregators
metrics: Gross landed price spread (22–45% net margin) between foreign distributor cost and US wholesale PO price
Inventory cash-conversion cycle (days from escrow release to US buyer wire settlement)
100% lot-level manufacturer authenticity verification and chain-of-custody pass rate

platform_risks.failure_mode: Brand-owner Lanham Act 'material difference' trademark challenge or marketplace invoice rejection
platform_risks.trigger: Importing foreign-language packaging or altered warranty/formulation SKUs that differ materially from the US domestic version
platform_risks.impact: CBP detention or Amazon brand-gating suppression on specific ASINs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Pre-purchase SKU inspection confirming identical UPC/EAN, multi-language compliant labeling, and identical physical formulation
platform_risks.fallback: Trade strictly in globally identical universal-packaging SKUs (duty-free prestige fragrances, universal OEM consumables) and sell primarily via direct B2B purchase orders to off-price retail chains and regional wholesalers rather than single-account Amazon storefronts

operator_plays.name: Certificate-of-Need (CON) & Decommissioned Hospital Imaging-Suite Arbitrage
operator_plays.mechanism: Acquire or option decommissioned imaging assets where approved site capacity has value, separating equipment resale economics from nontransferable or change-of-control-sensitive CON authority.
inputs: State CON decisions and hospital closure notices
Equipment service logs and site engineering surveys
Regulatory transfer guidance and buyer commitments
workflow: 1. Identify closing imaging suites and inventory equipment, permits, and lease rights
2. Confirm CON status, transfer restrictions, radiation licensing, and deinstallation costs
3. Negotiate approval-contingent asset purchases with qualified operators and equipment buyers
4. Close after regulatory clearance and document certified removal, installation, and acceptance

platform_risks.failure_mode: CON authority lapses or cannot transfer
platform_risks.trigger: Closure, relocation, or ownership change outside approved conditions
platform_risks.impact: Loss of site premium and stranded equipment carrying costs
platform_risks.detection_metric: Outstanding regulatory conditions and days to permit expiry
platform_risks.fallback: Exit under approval contingencies or sell inspected equipment separately without representing transferable operating authority

positioning_alternatives.title: The Removal-Ready Surplus Operator
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Turn federal and municipal surplus into collected B2B resale proceeds through disciplined bidding, scheduled removal, and documented asset condition.
positioning_alternatives.audience: A two-full-time, three-contractor operating pod with $15,000–$80,000 in startup capital, dependable freight access, and practical experience inspecting commercial equipment.
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: 40 U.S.C. 545 and 41 CFR Part 102-38 establish the federal surplus-sale framework. Individual auction terms determine inspection access, payment obligations, and removal deadlines. The positioning emphasizes execution risk rather than assumed auction discounts; municipal sales require separate review of the seller's authority and published terms.

positioning_alternatives.title: The Title-Ready Fleet Remarketer
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Build a repeatable vehicle-and-trailer resale operation around VIN verification, SF-97 documentation, repair ceilings, and qualified business buyers.
positioning_alternatives.audience: Fleet-service operators and equipment resellers with towing capacity, title-processing experience, and sufficient liquidity to carry vehicles through repair and registration delays.
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: Federal disposal rules provide the sale framework, while state vehicle law controls dealer licensing and title-transfer duties. California Vehicle Code sections 11700 and 5900 illustrate separate licensing and transfer-notice requirements. An SF-97 supports an application for state title; it is not itself a state-issued title or proof of roadworthiness.

positioning_alternatives.title: The Buyer-Led Industrial Surplus Desk
positioning_alternatives.subtitle: Source unrestricted shop equipment and commercial fixtures against documented B2B demand, with landed-cost bid ceilings and explicit disposition plans.
positioning_alternatives.audience: Industrial distributors, maintenance-service businesses, and small warehouse operators that already know local business buyers and can test equipment before remarketing.
positioning_alternatives.research_basis: The federal sales framework supports disciplined asset selection, but surplus status does not remove export controls or contractual restrictions. 15 CFR 736.2 and 22 CFR 121.1 provide relevant export-control references. California Revenue and Taxation Code section 6071 supplies a concrete example of a state seller-permit requirement.

chapters.title: What Exactly Is Government Surplus Auctions?
chapters.subtitle: GSA, GovPlanet, GovDeals and Public Surplus: Title Chains, SF-97, DEMIL Controls and B2B Resale Spreads
chapters.executive_summary: Government surplus auctions turn public-sector asset disposal into a disciplined inventory-resale business. Candidate #17, Pipeline Rank #29 of 29, scores 79/100 because transport, working capital, inspection and removal labor constrain leverage. This chapter maps six operating plays: distressed_asset_recovery, fleet title arbitrage, industrial equipment remarketing, institutional furniture bundling, parts harvesting and scheduled buyer matching. The latter five are chapter-level implementations, not additional catalog identifiers. Recognized operator revenue is gross resale proceeds when acting as principal; acquisition, hauling and refurbishment remain costs. Canonical annual owner profits are $12,000 Conservative, $80,500 Base and $200,000 Scaled. Durable operators win through inspection evidence, clean transfer documents, predictable removal and repeat commercial buyers, rather than spectacular auction screenshots.

sections.heading: 1. Define the inventory business before choosing an auction platform
paragraphs: Government surplus auctions are a disposal channel, not a single asset class or a procurement contracting strategy. A public agency sells vehicles, machinery, furniture or other property it no longer needs; an operator purchases selected lots, completes removal, improves marketability and resells to a different buyer population. Federal public sales operate within authorities including 40 U.S.C. 545 and 41 CFR Part 102-38. Municipal sellers follow their own applicable disposal authorities and sale documents. GSA Auctions and GSA Fleet Sales provide federal channels; GovDeals and Public Surplus host many local-government sellers. GovPlanet offers equipment auctions, including certain government-origin assets, but platform identity alone does not establish the seller, asset history or transfer restrictions. Read the actual lot terms. This business differs from buying tax liens, pursuing unclaimed funds or bidding to supply agencies under the FAR. Its basic product is usable equipment delivered with credible condition evidence and transferable rights. The operator earns the difference between an inconvenient public disposal transaction and a useful commercial purchase. That difference must pay for inspection, capital, hauling, repairs, storage, selling effort and mistakes before it becomes owner profit. A low winning bid is only the opening entry in that calculation.

The revenue boundary follows the operator's role in the resale transaction. A principal that controls purchased inventory before transfer to its customer generally recognizes gross resale proceeds when the applicable revenue-recognition conditions are satisfied. Buying an asset for $14,000 and selling it for $23,000 creates $23,000 of resale revenue, not $9,000 of revenue and not $37,000 of transaction volume. Purchase cost, buyer premium, transport and refurbishment belong in the cost structure, with inventory accounting determining their timing. Customer deposits received before performance are not automatically earned revenue. Sales tax collected for a taxing authority is excluded from revenue; expected returns and price concessions also affect the amount recognized. By contrast, an agent arranging another owner's $23,000 sale for a $2,300 commission generally recognizes its $2,300 fee rather than the underlying asset value. Merely taking payment does not settle the principal-versus-agent analysis. Document control, performance obligations, inventory exposure and pricing responsibility. The canonical scorecard uses principal resale proceeds, so combining brokerage GMV with owned-inventory revenue would inflate throughput and destroy margin comparability. Maintain separate ledger accounts for owned stock, consigned stock, customer deposits, collected taxes and earned service fees.

Choose a narrow operating archetype before opening dozens of auction alerts. Fleet specialists understand VIN verification, title packets, odometer disclosures and the commercial buyers for specific vehicle configurations. Industrial equipment traders know power requirements, attachment compatibility, loading geometry and the cost of proving operation. Institutional furniture traders win through standardized sets, measured dimensions and economical delivery, not through individual chairs with attractive photographs. Technology recovery operators need asset identification, sanitization evidence and a lawful downstream route for batteries and unusable components. Parts specialists require model-level demand knowledge and a documented disposition path for residual material. These are different businesses even when the same municipality supplies inventory. Start with one category, one removal radius and two reachable buyer segments. The stated startup capital range is $15,000 to $80,000, monthly operating expense range is $3,000 to $15,000, and first-deal window is one to six months. Those ranges describe the opportunity, not permission to spend the maximum before proving sell-through. Reserve money for unloading, unexpected repairs and slow collections rather than committing the entire account to hammer prices. A repeatable buyer conversation is more valuable than a broad watchlist because it defines the specifications worth purchasing and the defects that make a cheap lot unusable.

sections.heading: 2. Underwrite the asset, transfer documents and removal obligation together
paragraphs: Auction platforms provide access, but the seller's contract determines the actual purchase. Capture the lot description, photographs, amendments, inspection rules, payment instructions, buyer premium, tax treatment and removal deadline before submitting a bid. Fees vary by seller, sale and lot; never transfer a remembered GovDeals percentage to Public Surplus or assume every GSA-related sale has identical charges. Build a worksheet that distinguishes hammer price, percentage premium, fixed transaction charges, applicable taxes and conditional export or document costs. Obtain a written hauling quote identifying loading responsibility, equipment dimensions, estimated weight, appointment restrictions and whether the site supplies a functioning forklift. A truck reservation without a loading plan is not a removal plan. Inspection should target expensive uncertainty: cold starts, hour-meter plausibility, hydraulic leaks, battery condition, accessories and missing controllers. Photographs can establish configuration without establishing operability. If inspection is unavailable, price the lot against an evidenced downside exit rather than an optimistic repair estimate. Do not assume an as-is seller must refund a disappointing purchase. Dispute rights, abandonment consequences and payment-default remedies depend on the applicable terms and law. Preserve correspondence and ask specific questions early enough that the answers can change the bid rather than merely explain a loss.

Vehicle paperwork and restricted-property controls require separate diligence because mechanical condition cannot cure a defective transfer path. An SF-97, United States Government Certificate to Obtain Title to a Vehicle, is evidence used in obtaining a state title; it is not itself a state title or proof that every vehicle qualifies for road registration. Compare the VIN on the asset, listing, invoice and transfer documents, then confirm the receiving state's requirements for that vehicle category before bidding. Odometer disclosure requirements under 49 CFR Part 580 apply subject to their scope and exemptions. Salvage history, missing supporting documents and off-road design can change the resale audience. Separately, military-origin equipment may carry demilitarization, end-use, export or disposal conditions. Record the applicable DEMIL information and sale-specific obligations; do not infer unrestricted status from camouflage, platform branding or a seller's casual description. The U.S. Munitions List in 22 CFR 121.1 and export prohibitions in 15 CFR Part 736 illustrate distinct control systems that can require classification work. Use a qualified specialist for restricted categories and exclude lots whose lawful possession, transfer or required processing cannot be established. A prospective foreign buyer does not resolve the seller's export responsibilities.

The comparison matrix separates attractive demand from operational fit. Portable generators may have broad contractor demand, yet load testing and fuel-system work can exceed the expected spread. Laboratory equipment can appear valuable against original purchase price while missing software licenses, probes or calibration records. School furniture often sells in quantities that overwhelm a small warehouse even when the per-unit purchase price looks trivial. For each sub-vertical, record three independent facts: a comparable completed sale, a buyer's minimum acceptable specification and a credible removal quote. Treat asking prices as leads rather than valuation evidence. Favor routes where one outbound truck can serve several buyers or where repeat buyers collect inspected inventory themselves. Maintain a dated lot file in Airtable or a spreadsheet, with invoices and inspection photographs linked through stable asset identifiers. Track bid-to-win rate, landed-cost variance, days to ready-for-sale and days to collected payment. A category with modest spreads and reliable forty-day cash conversion can outperform a spectacular-looking machine held for a year. Establish disposition deadlines before purchase: retail listing first, specialist wholesale offer second, verified parts or scrap outlet last. The fallback should be executable with current buyers and transport capacity, not simply described as selling it somewhere else.

callout.title: Buy evidence before buying equipment
callout.body: Veteran operators reduce uncertainty before the auction clock makes haste feel productive.
items: Ask the custodian to photograph the data plate, electrical panel and missing-accessory areas; generic exterior photographs rarely answer the expensive questions.
Quote freight using actual loading conditions, not mileage alone; explicitly identify who supplies ramps, rigging, forklift capacity and appointment coordination.
Request a sample of the promised vehicle document packet with sensitive fields removed, then confirm the document type with the receiving motor-vehicle agency.
Record completed-sale comparables by configuration and condition; an asking price for a tested machine cannot support a bid on an untested incomplete unit.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile gross resale proceeds to the three owner-profit cases
paragraphs: The canonical Conservative case is $150,000 of annual gross resale revenue at an 8% net margin, producing $12,000 of annual owner net profit with two full-time people and three contractors. Base is $575,000 at 14.0%, producing $80,500 with the same stated team structure. Scaled is $1,000,000 at 20%, producing $200,000 with three full-time people and four contractors, seven people total. The corresponding total annual cost envelopes are $138,000, $494,500 and $800,000. These are the scorecard cases, not additive revenue streams or automatic results from hiring those teams. Contractor counts do not imply full-year utilization, and headcount alone does not establish affordable payroll. Build an explicit labor budget covering employee wages, employer costs, contractor invoices and the treatment of working-owner compensation. Do not silently remove labor to preserve a target margin. If measured staffing expense and other costs exceed a case's cost envelope, that case is operationally infeasible under those assumptions. Likewise, owner profit is not a promise that every listed team member receives that amount. The scorecard's capital-intensive designation reflects inventory funding, physical handling and limited automation leverage. Evaluate both earnings and cash tied up, because a profitable resale booked late does not fund tomorrow's auction payment.

A worked lot illustrates the Base arithmetic without changing the annual targets. Assume $23,000 of recognized resale proceeds, a $14,000 hammer price, an illustrative 10% buyer premium of $1,400, $900 transport, $1,500 refurbishment and $600 direct handling. Those costs total $18,400, leaving $4,600 before allocated overhead. Allocate another $1,380 of operating expense to produce $3,220 of modeled owner profit, exactly 14% of revenue. Twenty-five identical completed sales yield $575,000 revenue and $80,500 profit. This is a mathematical bridge, not evidence that twenty-five real lots will carry identical costs or support the stated staffing. The premium is an example, not a published platform rate. Test the overhead allocation against actual payroll, rent, insurance, selling expenses, carrying costs and expected losses. For bidding, solve backward: a $23,000 expected sale less $3,220 required profit, $900 transport, $1,500 refurbishment, $600 handling and $1,380 overhead leaves $15,400 for hammer plus premium. With only a 10% premium applicable, the hammer ceiling is $14,000. Additional nonrecoverable taxes or charges reduce that ceiling. Never increase the resale estimate merely because another bidder crosses the calculated limit.

Cash conversion makes the same margin either manageable or dangerous. In the worked example, the $14,000 hammer, $1,400 premium, $900 hauling and $1,500 refurbishment consume $17,800 before handling and overhead. Four overlapping lots therefore require $71,200 for those components alone, well beyond the low end of the startup capital range. Customer payment terms can extend the funding gap after delivery, so separate days held from days awaiting collection. A hypothetical $1,000 repair overrun reduces the worked lot's $3,220 profit to $2,220; a further $2,000 selling-price reduction leaves only $220. Track these sensitivities before accepting thin spreads on uninspected equipment. Inventory aging should trigger an action, such as fresh condition evidence, a different buyer channel or an executable wholesale quote, rather than indefinite optimism. Maintain a weekly cash calendar with auction settlement, removal, repair authorization, payroll and expected customer receipts. Reserve disposal and transport money even for unsuccessful lots. The monthly operating expense range does not replace a cash budget, and inventory purchases are not interchangeable with recurring overhead. Reconcile each asset's realized proceeds and complete cost record to the general ledger; aggregate margin improves only when individual losses remain visible rather than being buried inside the next purchase.

sections.heading: 4. Build six repeatable plays around evidence, buyers and cash discipline
paragraphs: The catalog play distressed_asset_recovery, Distressed Asset Recovery under TRACK_1, applies here as acquisition spread on administratively inconvenient surplus, not as a claim that the operator owns public money awaiting recovery. Consider an eligible equipment lot bought for $2,800 with a $280 illustrative premium, $600 hauling and $400 preparation. At a $5,000 resale, the $920 contribution before overhead falls to $580 after $340 allocated overhead. The edge is resolving description, access or buyer-matching friction without assuming hidden legal rights. The broader play's fallback is diversification across multi-state dockets and attorney-backed filing partnerships where required; those recovery-fee activities need separate authority, contracts and revenue accounts rather than being blended into auction resale totals. The second chapter-level implementation, fleet title arbitrage, means buying a vehicle whose documented transfer route and useful configuration are undervalued, not manufacturing or bypassing title evidence. An $8,000 purchase, $800 premium, $1,200 repairs and $700 hauling against a $12,000 resale leave $1,300 before overhead. If registration eligibility cannot be established, decline the lot. A lawful wholesale buyer can be a fallback for an eligible vehicle, but wholesaling cannot cure missing ownership rights or transfer restrictions.

Industrial equipment remarketing converts technical verification into a saleable specification. A $6,000 machine plus $600 premium, $900 rigging and $1,000 service costs $8,500 before overhead; a $10,500 resale leaves $2,000 contribution. Require a competent test of the functions the buyer actually needs, not merely a video showing an illuminated control panel. If repair economics deteriorate, seek a documented specialist wholesale quote before purchasing additional parts. Institutional furniture bundling uses a different advantage: consistent sets and dense transport. Twenty usable desks sold at $150 each generate $3,000 revenue. A $1,000 lot, $100 premium, $500 removal and $300 cleaning leave $1,100 contribution before overhead. Count usable pieces, confirm dimensions and photograph matching finishes before promising a bundle. If only twelve desks are usable, the same $1,900 costs against $1,800 revenue produce a $100 loss before overhead. These examples show why original procurement price is a poor bidding anchor. The real determinants are current functionality, completeness and the next buyer's alternatives. Neither implementation should absorb unlimited warehouse space: set a category-specific aging limit and a wholesale exit price that includes another round of loading and transport.

Parts harvesting and scheduled buyer matching complete the six-play operating map. Eligible equipment bought for $1,200 with $120 premium, $300 hauling and $500 dismantling costs $2,120. Eight tested components sold for $350 each generate $2,800, leaving $680 before overhead, selling fees, returns and residual disposal. Unsold components are inventory, not earned revenue. Reject restricted equipment and use documented material-recovery partners for remaining waste. Scheduled buyer matching instead starts with a buyer's written specification and delivery window. Ten eligible cabinets sold for $400 each generate $4,000; a $2,000 purchase, $200 premium, $600 hauling and $300 preparation leave $900 before overhead. Purchase as principal only when funding and alternate buyers survive cancellation; an agency arrangement would require fee-based revenue treatment. Automate auction alerts, bid-limit worksheets and inventory tracking, but keep condition judgments and transfer checks with accountable people. Weekly review should identify which buyer requests repeat, which sellers describe lots accurately and which transport routes remain economical. Durable moats accumulate in those records and relationships. Fragile beginner hype concentrates on winning bids, headline retail prices and gross transaction screenshots while ignoring elapsed time, incomplete equipment, unpaid labor and the cost of moving the same asset twice.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, ranks #29 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 79/100. The business earns gross resale proceeds, not government procurement budgets or customer purchasing principal. This chapter maps six plays: fleet resale, shop-equipment resale, municipal-equipment resale, parts-lot breakup, authorized buyer sourcing, and government_rfp_subcontractor_brokerage. The first five are chapter-local operating routes; the sixth is an adjacent procurement model with separate accounting. Buyers pay to restore productive capacity, secure scarce equipment, or meet contracted delivery obligations. Clean settlement requires verified purchasing authority, permitted payment rails, documented release conditions, and accurate title representations. sections.heading: 1. Identify the economic buyer, purchasing authority and reason to pay now
paragraphs: Government surplus contains two different check writers, and confusing them breaks both sales strategy and bookkeeping. At acquisition, your trading company pays the government seller or its authorized auction collection agent. At resale, a contractor, fleet owner, dealer, manufacturer, or qualified recycler pays your company for an identified asset. The agency disposing of equipment is usually your supplier, not your customer. Its pressures include storage expense, property accountability, and scheduled site clearance; none automatically creates a purchasing budget for your services. The downstream buyer's urgency is more measurable: a disabled truck can strand a crew, an unavailable compressor can stop production, and a missing attachment can delay a contracted job. Ask for the lost productive hours, the replacement rental quote, the required delivery date, and the person authorized to release funds. A buyer facing a $450 daily rental bill can rationally pay $1,800 above another seller's price for four days of earlier usable delivery, provided condition and transport are credible. That comparison establishes a negotiation ceiling, not extra recognized revenue until a sale occurs. Sell documented readiness rather than an auction bargain story.

Map authority before discussing deposits. A maintenance supervisor can confirm specifications without possessing spending authority; a controller can approve payment without accepting mechanical condition; a public purchasing officer may need an issued purchase order before any commitment binds the organization. Obtain the legal buyer name, billing address, authorized signatory, purchase-order requirement, tax documentation, and accounts-payable contact through independently checked channels. For a public buyer, establish the applicable purchasing method and delegated threshold rather than accepting a verbal promise that an invoice will be processed later. Do not divide invoices to evade purchasing limits. For financed equipment, the lender's conditions matter as much as the buyer's enthusiasm: serial verification, acceptable ownership documents, insurance, and an executed security agreement may precede funding. An escrow provider holds funds according to instructions; it does not create budget authority or cure an unauthorized purchase. Separate the buyer, payer, consignee, and beneficial business relationship whenever their names differ. A legitimate leasing company may pay for its customer, but the file must explain who owns the asset and who may collect it. Stop an unexplained third-party payment before it becomes a disputed delivery.

The strongest buyer interview tests the failure consequence, not merely the budget. A fleet operator values a transferable vehicle identity, a dealer values wholesale exit liquidity, and a recycler values recoverable material less processing and disposal expense. A buyer requesting regulated equipment may face licensing, export, or handling requirements, but those restrictions constrain the transaction rather than force a purchase. SF-97 is a federal certificate used to obtain vehicle title; it is not itself a state-issued title or permission to operate the vehicle. Confirm the issuing seller's document process and the destination motor-vehicle agency's requirements before promising registration. Likewise, a DEMIL designation must be interpreted against the specific lot, sale terms, and controlling agency requirements; a commercial auction listing does not erase destruction or end-use conditions. Qualify buyers for those conditions before collecting nonrefundable money. Use GSA Auctions for federal listings and review GovPlanet, GovDeals, and PublicSurplus listings at the seller-and-lot level, because platform presence does not establish uniform ownership, payment, or removal terms. The decisive sales document connects one buyer's operating problem to one deliverable asset, with evidence of condition, ownership route, delivery timing, and price.

sections.heading: 2. Choose the settlement rail by control, timing and release evidence
paragraphs: Start with the auction seller's accepted methods and deadlines, then design the downstream collection process around the resulting cash gap. Federal sale payment requirements appear in 41 CFR Part 102-38, Subpart D, while the actual invitation supplies transaction-specific terms. Municipal sellers and commercial auction operators use their own applicable conditions. Never promise escrow, installment settlement, or a credit-card payment unless that seller accepts it for that lot and amount. Read the hammer-price basis, buyer premium, tax treatment, payment deadline, removal deadline, default provisions, and refund process together. A $6,000 hammer price plus a 10% buyer premium produces a $6,600 acquisition invoice before any applicable tax or other charge; it does not establish your customer's resale price. Verify bank instructions through a known platform session or independently obtained seller contact, especially after any emailed change. Send the correct invoice reference and retain the bank's transaction identifier. A payment screenshot proves only that somebody produced an image. Release requires the seller's or your bank's appropriate confirmation, reconciled to the right account and invoice, plus completion of any document conditions.

The eight methods below are not interchangeable settlement systems. Wire and ACH move funds; platform checkout orchestrates supported methods; escrow and milestone holds allocate performance risk; retainers fund defined services; factoring advances against eligible receivables; statutory disbursement describes payment governed by a public contracting framework. For an unfamiliar buyer collecting a high-value machine, a verified domestic wire may fit better than an ACH debit because debit authorization and return exposure can outlast apparent availability. Wires still carry fraud, mistaken-payment, and legal recovery risks; never describe any rail as immune to dispute. Ask the bank to explain the relevant settlement status rather than inventing a universal waiting period. Escrow works only when the provider accepts the asset type, both parties execute consistent instructions, and release evidence is objective. Define serial numbers, inspection location, acceptance window, transport responsibility, dispute procedure, and fee allocation. A vague promise to release when the buyer is happy invites delay. Milestone holds can protect a downstream installation customer but usually cannot rewrite the upstream auction's payment deadline. Fund that mismatch with committed capital, not an expectation that the auctioneer will extend terms.

Public-contract payment timing belongs in a separate lane from auction settlement. For qualifying federal procurement, the Prompt Payment Act and 5 CFR Part 1315 govern payment administration, with contract terms and applicable FAR clauses determining invoice and acceptance mechanics. They do not require GSA to finance your surplus purchase or guarantee that a prime contractor pays your brokerage invoice immediately. If factoring supports a service contract, establish an eligible receivable, verify assignment restrictions, and obtain the required notices and acknowledgments before counting an advance. Federal assignment rules under 31 U.S.C. § 3727 and 41 U.S.C. § 6305 can materially constrain the arrangement; a generic commercial factoring form is insufficient. A $20,000 eligible invoice with an 85% advance produces $17,000 of initial liquidity, while the remaining $3,000 is a reserve before fees and adjustments, not new sales. For authorized sourcing services, a $750 retainer credited against a $1,500 earned sourcing fee is part payment of that fee, not additional auction revenue. Record refundable deposits as liabilities until the relevant performance and accounting conditions are met. Reconcile every receipt to its contractual role before measuring margin.

sections.heading: 3. Protect the spread and separate six mapped operating plays
paragraphs: The canonical scorecard recognizes gross resale proceeds, with acquisition, transport, and refurbishment inside the margin. Conservative is $150,000 revenue less $138,000 total costs, yielding $12,000 annual owner net profit at 8%; Base is $575,000 less $494,500, yielding $80,500 at 14.0%; Scaled is $1,000,000 less $800,000, yielding $200,000 at 20%. Teams remain 2 FT + 3 C, 2 FT + 3 C, and 3 FT + 4 C respectively. An illustrative Base construction is 50 annual sales averaging $11,500. Per sale, allocate $6,000 purchase, $600 buyer premium, $850 transport, $700 refurbishment, $230 selling expense, $110 payment expense, and $1,400 remaining operating costs. Those costs total $9,890, leaving $1,610; multiplying both sides by 50 reproduces the Base totals exactly. The allocation is a planning example, not a claim that every lot has identical economics. Include unrecoverable acquisition taxes and realized defect losses within actual costs, and avoid counting sales tax collected for remittance as resale revenue. The monthly opex range of $3,000–$15,000 is a cash-planning input, not an extra deduction layered onto already fully costed scenario margins. Reconcile classifications before changing any profit figure.

Five chapter-local routes translate that resale engine into specific buyer propositions: fleet resale, shop-equipment resale, municipal-equipment resale, parts-lot breakup, and authorized buyer sourcing. These labels organize this chapter; they are not additional canonical scorecard candidates. The first four can involve ownership and gross resale recognition when the operator acts as principal. Authorized sourcing can instead be an agency service, in which only the earned fee is revenue and customer purchasing principal remains separately tracked. Do not combine that fee-only activity with the canonical gross resale projection without a separate reconciliation. Protect margin through a signed offer identifying the asset, condition exceptions, inspection rights, delivery scope, taxes, payment deadline, and release documents. For a sourcing engagement, define what earns the fee: a documented search, an authorized acquisition, or another objective deliverable. Record introduced counterparties and use a reasonable, specifically scoped non-circumvention provision where enforceable; never rely on secrecy to hide publicly listed auction stock. Avoid bidding from a customer's credentials or collecting platform charges outside permitted channels. When a customer can purchase directly, sell inspection, logistics, and execution value, not an invented exclusive right to access government inventory.

The sixth mapped play, government_rfp_subcontractor_brokerage, is adjacent procurement rather than surplus resale. Monitor federal SAM.gov opportunities, state procurement portals, and municipal bid boards through permitted feeds or rate-conscious collection for low-bid-density janitorial, grounds, courier, translation, and IT staffing solicitations. Use proposal automation to assemble requirements and evidence, while people validate scope, wage obligations, qualifications, and subcontractor capacity. A $100,000 service contract with $75,000 fulfillment cost creates a $25,000 management spread, or 25% of contract revenue, before proposal expense, insurance, supervision, financing, and other overhead. It is not $25,000 net profit and does not augment the surplus scorecard automatically. A 15–30% target spread requires credible delivery economics, not merely an inexpensive subcontractor. For covered service set-asides, 13 CFR § 125.6 generally limits payments to firms that are not similarly situated to 50% of the amount paid by the government, subject to the rule's applicability and exclusions. Review further subcontracting and the applicable measurement period. If the delivery structure fails, bid unrestricted commercial or municipal work without those federal set-aside caps, or team exclusively with qualified similarly situated entities while still satisfying applicable performance rules.

sections.heading: 4. Screen credit, control release and close the cash-to-custody loop
paragraphs: Counterparty screening should answer whether this entity can pay, whether this person can bind it, and whether this particular transaction makes commercial sense. Check the business registry, operating address, domain history when relevant, independent phone contact, trade references, and consistency between purchase documents and bank remitter. Obtain appropriate credit information with required authorization and check public liens or bankruptcy records when exposure justifies it. A UCC filing can reveal an existing secured credit relationship, but its presence does not establish insolvency and its absence does not prove creditworthiness. Request recent accounts or a lender commitment for material deferred exposure instead of interpreting a polished website as liquidity. Begin unfamiliar accounts with payment before release, and extend terms only against a documented limit, collection process, and loss capacity. If financed resale uses a security interest, determine attachment and perfection under the applicable state's enacted Article 9 and any certificate-of-title rules. A generic retention of title sentence may not protect the seller against competing creditors. Keep credit approval separate from the salesperson's commission incentive, and record who accepted each exception and the maximum dollars exposed.

Run the transaction through one lot-level record from bid approval to final collection. Store the original listing, terms, bid limit, inspection notes, serial photographs, invoice, payment confirmation, ownership documents, buyer agreement, carrier authorization, and delivery acknowledgment. Auction alerts identify opportunities; bid-limit worksheets enforce downside assumptions; inventory tracking connects cash with physical custody. A spreadsheet or Airtable register can hold these fields, while QuickBooks tracks invoices and costs using the same lot identifier. Automation should flag exceptions rather than silently release equipment. A freight carrier arriving early does not waive payment conditions. Match the driver's collection authority to the approved carrier and lot, confirm loading arrangements, and capture pickup evidence without unnecessarily retaining personal identity documents. For restricted property, complete required screening and seller-prescribed end-use, export, or demilitarization procedures before transfer. Do not assume disassembly converts controlled equipment into unrestricted parts. If the asset or buyer cannot satisfy the stated conditions, decline the acquisition or use an expressly authorized disposal route. Removal deadlines create operational urgency, but urgency never grants permission to change payment recipients, forge release records, or bypass property restrictions.

Manage working capital as a dated schedule rather than an annual profit percentage. In the Base illustration, acquisition, premium, transport, and refurbishment consume $8,150 per unit before selling and remaining operating costs. Four overlapping units therefore tie up $32,600 before those additional expenses, even though their eventual combined modeled profit is only $6,440. Compare that requirement with the canonical $15,000–$80,000 startup capital range and a realistic first-deal horizon of 1–6 months. A refundable buyer deposit reduces immediate cash pressure only while the corresponding refund obligation remains funded; it is not free equity. Establish aging reviews tied to actual carrying cost and exit bids, with named responsibility for repricing or liquidation. After delivery, reconcile gross invoice proceeds, tax liabilities, payment charges, transport, repairs, credits, and released deposits against the lot record. Investigate overpayments instead of forwarding the difference to an unrelated account; route legitimate refunds through a verified original payment relationship. Close only when ownership documentation, funds, custody, and remaining obligations agree. The operator's durable advantage is not winning more auctions; it is converting selected assets into collected, fully costed sales without losing control of the release.

chapters.question_prompt: What are the real unit economics, gross-to-net margin deductions, scrub/reversal reserves, and working-capital float requirements for government surplus auctions?
chapters.title: Unit Economics, Margin Waterfall & Working-Capital Float
chapters.subtitle: GSA, GovDeals, GovPlanet and PublicSurplus Cohorts: SF-97 Title Costs, DEMIL Screens, Contractor Labor and Cash-Release Timing
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, holds Rank #29 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score because capital turns and physical execution constrain apparently attractive auction spreads. Canonical annual owner profits are $12,000 Conservative, $80,500 Base, and $200,000 Scaled, on gross resale proceeds rather than commissions or underlying asset valuations. This chapter maps six operating plays: fleet-vehicle remarketing, municipal equipment bundling, tested IT resale, industrial-parts harvesting, buyer-backed wholesale lots, and allocation-arbitrage screening. These are editorial operating mappings, not additional scorecard candidates. The waterfall prices purchase premiums, freight, repair, contractor delivery, customer acquisition, selling fees, reversal exposure, and fixed overhead. Cash calendars then expose payment-before-removal requirements, buyer receivables, payout holds, and the liquidity required to survive slower exits without forced liquidation.

sections.heading: 1. Price the Entire Cohort Before Setting a Hammer Limit
paragraphs: Treat the acquisition cohort, not the winning bid, as the economic unit. A cohort contains assets purchased together, their removal jobs, refurbishment work orders, buyer invoices, and eventual cash releases. The illustrative annual plans below use thirty Conservative cohorts averaging $5,000 resale proceeds, one hundred Base cohorts averaging $5,750, and one hundred sixty Scaled cohorts averaging $6,250. Those volumes are planning assumptions; the revenue, margin, profit, and staffing totals are the canonical scorecard. Revenue is gross operator resale proceeds from owned inventory, never the government's original acquisition value or a buyer's subsequent resale. The chapter does not substitute a commission business for an inventory business. Capture GSA Auctions, GovDeals, PublicSurplus, and GovPlanet terms separately: seller identity, premium, accepted payment method, pickup window, and title documentation can differ by listing. Save the listing and invoice in an immutable lot folder before payment. Establish the bid ceiling from documented exit comparables and written transport quotes, then deduct every downstream cost. A winning bid above that ceiling is an underwriting error even when the asset looks inexpensive beside its original procurement price.

The Base cohort makes the deduction sequence concrete. Begin with $5,750 gross resale proceeds and subtract $2,530 hammer cost, $201.25 acquisition premium, $345 inbound transport, $287.50 refurbishment, $230 contractor delivery labor, $115 customer acquisition, $172.50 selling and payment fees, and $115 expected scrub or reversal losses. Contribution is $1,753.75 before $948.75 allocated fixed expense, leaving $805 owner profit. Multiply each line by one hundred and the annual waterfall reaches exactly $80,500. The premium assumption is a blended budget, not a published platform rate. Contractor delivery covers inspection coordination, handover, and dispatch hours; inbound transport pays the carrier, preventing the same invoice from entering both buckets. Refurbishment includes parts and bench work, while fixed payroll covers recurring operating roles. Customer acquisition means attributable buyer prospecting and paid lead generation, not the auction purchase price. State sales tax collected for remittance is outside revenue; recoverable tax is outside expense. Nonrecoverable purchase tax belongs inside acquisition cost and reduces the permitted hammer price. Reconcile resale certificates against the seller's actual acceptance rules before assuming a tax-free purchase.

Do not mistake the staffing labels for fully salaried positions funded at every scale. The Conservative illustration assigns both full-time roles to working owners and budgets $21,000 for fixed operating expense, with owner labor compensated only through the $12,000 residual. That is economically weak and unsuitable as a replacement-income plan for two people. The Base illustration assigns one full-time owner and one employee, with $60,000 loaded employee cost and $34,875 other fixed expense. Scaled assigns one owner and two employees, with $120,000 loaded employee cost and $60,000 other fixed expense. Contractor counts describe available specialists, not continuously purchased full-time equivalents. These allocations explain the scorecard rather than assert local wage feasibility. Obtain actual wage, insurance, storage, and payroll-tax quotes before deployment. Owner profit here is the operating residual before owner-level income taxes and any additional debt expense; it includes compensation for owner work. Replacement-manager cost would reduce it. The $3,000–$15,000 monthly operating range is a cash-planning context, not an extra deduction pasted onto already allocated expenses. Map every cash invoice to one waterfall bucket and reconcile financing separately if borrowing is used.

callout.title: Protect the Spread Before the Auction Closes
callout.body: Experienced buyers improve certainty before raising bid limits; the worksheet must preserve evidence as well as arithmetic.
items: Obtain a removal quote using the actual loading dock, forklift availability, asset weight, and appointment window; attach the carrier's accessorial schedule.
Ask the seller which vehicle document will be issued and when; price a delayed SF-97 as additional holding time rather than assuming immediate retail title.
Keep separate carrier and contractor task codes so loading, dispatch, and handover charges cannot quietly enter the waterfall twice.
Use sold comparables with matching condition and buyer freight terms; an asking price with free delivery is not an equivalent cash exit.

sections.heading: 2. Map Six Plays Without Importing Artificial Allocation Advantages
paragraphs: Five physical-surplus plays translate directly into acquisition discipline. Fleet-vehicle remarketing buys a documented truck for $8,000, adds $3,000 acquisition and preparation costs, and targets $13,000 resale, creating $2,000 contribution before fixed expense and losses. Municipal equipment bundling combines three compatible mowers costing $2,400 with $900 execution expense and a $4,200 buyer commitment, leaving $900. Tested IT resale places twenty desktops at $120 acquisition plus $45 testing and selling cost each, then exits at $210 each for $900 aggregate contribution. Industrial-parts harvesting pays $1,500 for a permissible assembly, budgets $700 dismantling and selling expense, and collects $3,000 across identified parts, leaving $800. Buyer-backed wholesale lots spend $6,000 on inventory and $1,000 execution against an $8,000 documented exit, leaving $1,000. These examples are bid-screening illustrations, not additional revenue layered onto the canonical scenarios. Each requires an evidence-backed fallback: licensed wholesale vehicle disposal, individual mower sales, tested component recovery, permitted scrap disposition, or a second wholesale buyer. Deduct the fallback's actual removal and selling costs before treating its quoted price as recoverable cash. Never add incompatible exit alternatives together.

The sixth mapping is allocation-arbitrage screening, including the supplied play identifier verified_fan_ticketing_and_drop_allocation_farming. Its proposed account multiplication is not an underwriting assumption for government surplus. Do not use fabricated identities, proxy rotation, or payment instruments to bypass bidder eligibility, purchase limits, or platform controls. Ticketmaster Verified Fan, AXS, U.S. Mint releases, and collectible drops also have different transfer and refund economics from physical surplus. A simple independent-draw illustration shows the capital problem without endorsing circumvention: twenty genuinely eligible participants with a ten percent allocation chance produce two expected allocations, not twenty certain fills. At $500 purchase cost, $650 resale, and $75 execution cost per allocation, expected contribution is $150 before coordination expense, while maximum purchase exposure could reach $10,000 if every participant succeeds. Actual selection events may be correlated, so this expectation is not a liquidity limit. Use only genuinely independent buyers acting within applicable rules, with transferable goods and valid buyer commitments. Distinct addresses or card details do not create permission. Where coordination or transfer is prohibited, the fallback is no participation, not a more elaborate account structure.

Eligibility and disposition restrictions must become dollar deductions or explicit reasons to reject a lot. For federal personal-property sales, start with 41 CFR Part 102-38 and the sale's incorporated terms; municipal platforms host different sellers and do not create one universal federal contract. For vehicles, an SF-97 documents a federal transfer for titling purposes but is not itself a state-issued title. Confirm the receiving state's documentation, inspections, fees, and dealer-license requirements before forecasting a retail exit. A $180 document correction plus twenty extra storage days at $12 removes $420 from contribution. For defense-origin assets, use the actual DEMIL code, sale restrictions, end-use conditions, and current DLA instructions. A supposed $3,000 resale is worth no unrestricted resale revenue when the authorized disposition requires destruction instead. Export controls under 15 CFR Parts 730–774 require classification and destination screening when applicable; defense articles can fall under a different regime. Do not infer unrestricted export from a successful auction purchase. Preserve serial numbers, disposition evidence, and buyer representations, and reject lots whose required documentation cannot be obtained before the binding payment deadline.

callout.title: Four Pre-Bid Verifications That Must Produce Evidence
callout.body: A spreadsheet margin is usable only after the underlying rights, costs, and cash commitments are established.
items: Verify bidder eligibility, purchase limits, authorized account ownership, and any required end-use documentation against the specific sale terms.
Verify SF-97 availability or other title evidence, serial identity, liens where relevant, and the receiving state's transfer requirements.
Verify DEMIL and export restrictions using authoritative classification records; remove any unauthorized resale route from the valuation.
Verify a priced removal appointment and available cash covering purchase, premium, tax exposure, and the full delayed-collection interval.

sections.heading: 3. Reserve for Defects and Reversals Without Counting Cash Twice
paragraphs: Define a scrub as inventory removed from the intended sale channel because inspection, documentation, condition, or buyer requirements invalidate the original exit. Define a reversal as a refund, chargeback, price concession, or settlement reduction after a buyer transaction. Neither definition makes a government seller responsible for repairing an as-is asset. Auction terms may place inspection and removal risk entirely on the purchaser. The reserve therefore belongs in the buyer's economics before bidding. The canonical reconciliation uses expected annual loss budgets of $4,500, $11,500, and $15,000, respectively. At Base volume, $115 per cohort can be decomposed into $60 expected defect loss, $25 return logistics, $20 documentation correction, and $10 unrecovered payment disputes. These are model assumptions to replace with observed cohort data, not probabilities supplied by the platforms. Record both frequency and severity: a two percent incident rate with a $5,750 full loss already consumes $115 per cohort. Partial recoveries, salvage proceeds, and carrier reimbursements reduce severity only after collectability is supported. Keep salvage estimates separate from verified offers so optimistic recoveries cannot conceal a deteriorating purchasing process.

Use the waterfall as a management reconciliation rather than a shortcut around proper books. In actual reporting, customer refunds may reduce revenue, inventory write-downs may affect inventory expense, and dispute fees remain selling costs. Reclassify those amounts without deducting them again from the same operating residual. The model's gross resale basis presents all expected loss leakage in one visible planning line; it does not prescribe financial-statement presentation. A cash reserve is another distinct object: transferring $11,500 into a reserve bank subaccount does not create an additional $11,500 expense. Track expected loss, booked loss, and restricted cash in separate fields. A settlement hold also differs from a loss because recoverable money remains an asset while unavailable for the next purchase. Require lot-level reason codes for failed acceptance, shipping damage, missing accessories, title delay, and unauthorized listing claims. Review resolved cases monthly and open cases weekly. Increase prospective bid deductions when condition disputes concentrate in a seller or category; do not rewrite historical purchase costs to make the acquisition team appear more accurate. Preserve dated assumptions so the next cohort can be evaluated honestly.

Stress the entire annual plan with consistent mechanics. A ten percent resale markdown reduces revenue by $15,000, $57,500, and $100,000. If selling fees alone flex at three percent, three percent, and two-and-one-half percent, the resulting profit reductions are $14,550, $55,775, and $97,500. Owner profits become negative $2,550, $24,725, and $102,500. Hold all other costs constant for this stress, including the absolute reserve; otherwise the test hides operating rigidity. A separate repair shock equal to five percent of hammer purchases costs $3,600, $12,650, and $20,000, reducing baseline profits to $8,400, $67,850, and $180,000. Apply both shocks together and the outcomes are negative $6,150, $12,075, and $82,500. These are sensitivities, not replacements for the canonical cases. The practical response is lower hammer limits, earlier wholesale exits, and more selective condition categories. Adding volume to a negative contribution cohort increases the loss. When a seller refuses inspection, price the defect exposure explicitly or decline the lot. When projected contribution is positive but cash recovery is slow, evaluate the capital-days consumed before deciding that expansion improves owner economics.

sections.heading: 4. Fund the Payment-to-Release Gap Before Increasing Auction Volume
paragraphs: Build the cash calendar from the auction's payment deadline to cleared buyer funds, not from the date an online listing goes live. This model assumes no supplier credit: hammer cost, premium, transport, refurbishment, contractor delivery, and buyer acquisition are funded before collection. Their annual totals are $108,000 Conservative, $370,875 Base, and $580,000 Scaled. Selling fees are withheld from settlement and expected losses are supported by a separate liquidity buffer, so neither enters the precollection spending numerator again. Conservative timing assumes sixty days from payment to invoice, twenty-five days of buyer DSO, and five additional days awaiting released settlement. Base assumes forty, thirty, and five days; Scaled assumes thirty-five, twenty, and five. These produce ninety, seventy-five, and sixty funded days. DSO here ends when the buyer pays; payout-lock days start afterward. If a processor reports DSO through bank receipt, do not add the same hold twice. Buyer prepayments shorten exposure only when actually collected and available under the contract. Refundable deposits remain potential cash obligations rather than unrestricted profit available for unrelated inventory speculation.

Approximate steady-state inventory and collection float as annual precollection spending divided by 365 and multiplied by funded days. The resulting requirements are $26,630, $76,207, and $95,342, rounded to dollars. Add three months of fixed expense, respectively $5,250, $23,719, and $45,000, plus the separate $4,500, $11,500, and $15,000 loss-liquidity buffers. Total planning liquidity becomes $36,380, $111,426, and $155,342. These illustrative requirements fit within the stated $15,000–$80,000 startup range, but the range's low end does not fund every scenario. They exclude separately purchased warehouse equipment, security deposits, and launch losses, which require their own opening cash lines. Uniform annual spending also understates lumpy auction purchases. Maintain a thirteen-week cash forecast showing every scheduled auction payment, removal appointment, payroll run, buyer receipt, and settlement release. Test a simultaneous purchase of the two largest intended lots against the minimum bank balance. If the business cannot pay both without relying on an unreleased receipt, reduce bid exposure. Credit availability counts only after documenting the facility limit, borrowing conditions, interest cost, and lender treatment of aging inventory.

An extra fifteen funded days ties up approximately $4,438, $15,241, and $23,836 beyond the planned float. A permanent increase of that size funded at twelve percent annual interest adds about $533, $1,829, and $2,860 annual carrying expense. Those charges are incremental sensitivities, not costs already deducted in the canonical profit figures. A short isolated delay instead incurs interest only for its actual financed duration. Link auction alerts to available capital, not merely category keywords: a promising truck should not trigger another purchase while a prior truck lacks transferable documents. Use a protected bid-limit worksheet, inventory identifiers, and bank settlement imports to update committed cash every business day. SQLite or a controlled spreadsheet is sufficient if asset IDs reconcile across invoices, work orders, and payouts. Allocate contractor hours by completed task and compare realized acquisition cost per buying customer against the cohort's budget. At each weekly review, rank aging stock by recoverable contribution per additional capital-day. Sell a slow lot wholesale when its incremental holding cost exceeds the credible retail uplift, even if that requires admitting the original retail price was too optimistic.

sop_steps.title: Open the cohort evidence record
sop_steps.action: Assign one asset or lot identifier before placing a bid.
sop_steps.detail: Attach listing terms, condition evidence, premium schedule, tax treatment, removal quote, title documents, and restriction checks to that identifier.

sop_steps.title: Compute the maximum funded hammer price
sop_steps.action: Subtract all execution costs, expected losses, fixed allocation, and target profit from supported resale proceeds.
sop_steps.detail: Solve percentage-based premiums and fees algebraically; lower the result further when the thirteen-week forecast cannot carry the entire payment-to-release interval.

sop_steps.title: Authorize contractor tasks against measured completion
sop_steps.action: Issue separate work orders for carrier transport, bench repair, and delivery coordination.
sop_steps.detail: Require timestamped pickup evidence, serial-level inspection results, and buyer acceptance records; reconcile actual hours and invoices without duplicate cost coding.

sop_steps.title: Close the cohort only after settlement reconciliation
sop_steps.action: Match buyer invoices, refunds, fees, reserve usage, and cleared bank receipts.
sop_steps.detail: Compare realized profit and funded days against the original worksheet, update prospective assumptions, and keep unresolved claims visible after physical delivery.

chapters.pull_quote: A surplus spread becomes owner profit only after the asset moves, the deductions clear, and the cash is free to buy again.
action_checklist: Build a lot-level waterfall that reproduces $12,000, $80,500, and $200,000 annual owner profit before applying any alternative assumptions.
Set every hammer ceiling from condition-matched sold comparables, written removal costs, actual premium terms, and a documented fallback exit.
Separate working-owner compensation, employee payroll, contractor task charges, and carrier invoices so staffing claims match funded economics.
Verify bidder eligibility, SF-97 or other title evidence, DEMIL restrictions, and applicable export classifications before committing purchase cash.
Maintain distinct records for expected losses, booked reversals, reserve cash, buyer DSO, and post-payment settlement holds.
Run markdown, repair, and fifteen-day delay stresses through a thirteen-week cash forecast before increasing simultaneous auction exposure.

chapters.question_prompt: How do you allocate startup capital ($15,000–$80,000 USD) and configure a lean, low-opex ($3,000–$15,000 USD/mo) production stack without wasting cash on bloated overhead?
chapters.title: Startup Capital, Lean Infrastructure & Pre-Flight Stack
chapters.subtitle: Reserve-First Buying, GSA and Municipal Removal Rails, SF-97 Title Controls, and a Twelve-Layer Resale Stack
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, ranks #29 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 79/100: inventory and removal execution matter more than software. Allocate 55% of startup cash to protected working-capital float, buy narrow categories, and rent handling capacity against confirmed pickups. This chapter maps six operating plays: local equipment lot splitting, titled fleet resale, parts recovery, contractor-direct remarketing, deadline-driven clearance, and section_321_de_minimis_bonded_tariff_arbitrage. The cross-border play is a restricted research branch, not an assumed duty exemption. Canonical annual owner profits remain $12,000 Conservative, $80,500 Base, and $200,000 Scaled. A twelve-layer stack, explicit purchase ceilings, title controls, and removal verification protect cash while preserving the $3,000–$15,000 monthly operating envelope. Gross resale proceeds—not customer inventory value or claimed tariff savings—anchor the surplus scorecard.

sections.heading: 1. Protect the float before buying the first pallet
paragraphs: Start with a six-envelope treasury rather than a shopping list. Put 55% of committed startup capital into protected working-capital float, 25% into initial auction purchases, 8% into transport and removal, 5% into inspection and repair, 4% into entity and insurance setup, and 3% into systems and equipment. At $25,000, that means $13,750, $6,250, $2,000, $1,250, $1,000, and $750 respectively. At $200,000, the same envelopes become $110,000, $50,000, $16,000, $10,000, $8,000, and $6,000. These are cash allocation ceilings, not instructions to spend every envelope or expense deposits immediately. Keep float outside the routine bidding account, transfer only against an approved lot worksheet, and reconcile cash weekly. A $13,750 reserve covers about 4.6 months at $3,000 monthly overhead before inventory losses or exceptional repairs; it does not fund a six-month wait comfortably. The stated one-to-six-month first-deal window therefore requires early buyer interviews and small acquisitions. Define a reserve breach before bidding: after all committed payments, unencumbered cash must still cover the agreed overhead runway and one failed removal. If it cannot, reduce the lot size rather than relabeling inventory as available cash.

Separate the startup envelopes from the recurring operating envelope. An illustrative $3,000 monthly floor assigns $800 to shared storage, $450 to insurance, $150 to communications and software, $250 to bookkeeping, $450 to recurring inspection and selling travel, $300 to utilities and security, and $600 to fixed-cost contingency. Auction acquisition, lot-specific freight, outsourced repairs, payroll, and payment fees still require separate entries; the floor is not a complete business cost statement. Avoid a warehouse lease merely because the capital account looks healthy. Use a written short-term yard agreement that allows the actual asset class, customer collections, loading equipment, and insured custody. Verify zoning, access hours, drainage, fire restrictions, and whether damaged vehicles or batteries are prohibited. A cheap space that cannot admit a flatbed during the seller's removal window is expensive storage. Request insurance quotes against specific operations: owned inventory, goods in transit, premises liability, commercial driving, and employees where applicable. A carrier's cargo certificate does not establish that every purchased machine is covered at replacement value. Record deductibles, exclusions, limits, and the claim evidence required before accepting the first load. Bind coverage before custody begins, not after the auction closes.

Preserve the scorecard without pretending that headcount is free. Conservative recognizes $150,000 of gross resale proceeds, allows $138,000 of total costs, and produces $12,000 owner net profit at 8%. Base recognizes $575,000, allows $494,500 of costs, and produces $80,500 at 14.0%. Scaled recognizes $1,000,000, allows $800,000 of costs, and produces $200,000 at 20%. Teams remain 2 FT + 3 C, 2 FT + 3 C, and 3 FT + 4 C respectively. These are canonical scenarios, not proof that local wage quotes fit. At $36,000 annual fixed overhead, Conservative has only $102,000 left for acquisitions, payroll, freight, repairs, and every other cost. Base with $60,000 overhead leaves $434,500; Scaled with $180,000 overhead leaves $620,000. Put actual employee compensation and contractor invoices into those residual budgets before hiring. If the staffing interpretation or market wages breaks the allowance, flag the case as unvalidated rather than hiding unpaid labor. Model owner compensation consistently and separately identify distributions. Inventory purchases consume cash immediately but generally become expense through cost of goods sold when sold; a cash-flow statement and a profit statement must therefore travel together. Never add customer-owned merchandise to operator resale revenue.
