callout.title: Spend on information and removal, not auction excitement
callout.body: The cheapest loss is the lot rejected before bidding; the next cheapest is the lot liquidated before storage and repairs compound.
items: Ask the municipal custodian whether a forklift and qualified operator will actually be available during your booked pickup window; platform photographs do not establish loading assistance.
Photograph serial plates, attachments, meter readings, and missing components during inspection, then price the asset using completed transactions for that exact configuration.
Negotiate shared-yard access by occupied bay or pallet position and require written permission for buyer collections before moving inventory there.
Book a backup carrier and a direct wholesale buyer for the first heavy lot; compare both quotes with the auction's actual removal deadline before bidding.

sections.heading: 2. Install twelve lean layers, each with an exit path
paragraphs: Build the stack around a single lot identifier that survives purchase, pickup, repair, listing, sale, and payment. A useful format combines auction source, sale date, and seller lot number; never reuse a number because a listing expired. Put the identifier in the bid worksheet, bank transfer memo, photographs, repair authorization, and customer invoice. Start with Airtable Free for structured inventory and Google Sheets for calculations, but keep the authoritative quantity and cost records in one designated system. Duplicate spreadsheets create phantom stock and stale price floors. Use platform-native auction alerts from GSA Auctions, GovDeals, Public Surplus, and GovPlanet where offered; filter on radius, category, removal terms, and inspection availability rather than broad bargain keywords. Federal ownership, municipal ownership, and private consignments require different seller-document checks even when the interface looks similar. Automate reminders, not binding purchases: a human must verify condition evidence and the final bid ceiling. Store dated sale terms alongside the lot record because fees and pickup rules can differ between sellers on the same platform. Archive cancellation emails and revised collection instructions rather than overwriting the original evidence.

Treat the matrix prices as explicit budgeting references, not verified live quotations. Listed paid subscription references reflect commonly published U.S. tiers and require a current checkout check for price, tax, billing term, and feature changes before purchase. Free account access never means free transactions: auction premiums, card processing, listing charges, and storage are separate costs. A two-user Google Workspace Business Starter plan at the $7 reference rate costs $14 monthly on annual commitment; one Backblaze Computer Backup seat at the $9 monthly reference adds $9. An eBay Starter Store at $4.95 monthly with annual subscription brings those three references to $27.95 monthly before taxes, devices, transaction fees, and any other services. That is enough software for an early operator, but not a complete overhead budget. Use individual accounts, multifactor authentication, and owner-controlled recovery methods. A personal free password vault is not a substitute for managed team credential sharing. Keep banking permissions distinct from inventory editing and document the second-person callback procedure for changed wire instructions. An attacker changing a freight invoice can erase months of margin without ever touching the auction account.

Physical infrastructure deserves the same cancellation discipline as software. Buy basic identification and testing equipment only after choosing a category: a multimeter, label printer, camera, and known-good power leads may serve office equipment, while vehicles demand different inspection competence and tools. Rent forklifts, trailers, and liftgate trucks against scheduled collections instead of carrying idle equipment. U-Haul's advertised cargo-van base-rate reference is not a freight quote; mileage, fuel, protection, taxes, availability, payload, and prohibited cargo can make it unsuitable. Put the actual transport quotation into the worksheet and use a qualified carrier when dimensions or weight exceed the rental's limits. Maintain a clean receiving area with separate untested, repair, sale-ready, and sold-awaiting-collection positions. Photograph goods before unloading and record damage immediately. Check that local fire and storage rules permit batteries, fuel residues, and stacked goods. Back up inventory exports and documents outside the working device, then restore a sample record monthly. A backup subscription alone does not protect cloud-only records that its product never captures. Every paid layer must have a named owner, cancellation date, and measurable reason to exist.

sections.heading: 3. Map six plays to bid limits, not speculative revenue
paragraphs: Six chapter operating plays organize the budget; the first five are descriptive surplus workflows, while the supplied cross-border play retains its exact identifier. For local equipment lot splitting, assume ten tested units can sell for $300 each: $3,000 gross resale proceeds. Deduct $300 selling costs, $400 removal, $300 repairs, and $600 required contribution toward overhead and profit. That leaves $1,400 for hammer price plus premium. With a hypothetical 10% premium and a valid purchase-tax exemption, the hammer ceiling is $1,272.72 after rounding down. Without exemption, include purchase tax on the applicable taxable base and lower the ceiling. Obtain actual seller fee terms rather than assuming 10% across platforms. For contractor-direct remarketing, an illustrative $8,000 sale less $5,000 acquisition, $600 freight, $400 testing, and $200 collection cost yields $1,800 contribution before shared overhead. A buyer conversation is not a purchase order; validate machine specifications, electrical supply, delivery access, and payment authority. If the intended contractor withdraws, use two alternative trade buyers' cash offers to set the fallback bid. Do not buy ten obscure units because one prospective customer liked a photograph.

For titled fleet resale, suppose a vehicle sells for $15,000 after $10,000 acquisition, $800 transport, $1,200 repairs, and $500 combined title, inspection, and selling costs. The remaining $2,500 is lot contribution, not owner net profit. A further $2,500 transmission failure consumes it entirely. Require diagnostic evidence, VIN matching, odometer documentation where applicable, and a destination-state registration pathway before bidding. SF-97 is a U.S. Government Certificate to Obtain Title to a Vehicle; it supports an application and is not itself a state title. Ask the receiving motor vehicle agency which supporting documents, inspections, taxes, and signatures it requires. For parts recovery, eight tested assemblies selling at $250 each produce $2,000 proceeds. Subtract a $700 donor purchase, $300 dismantling labor, $200 freight, $200 selling costs, and $150 residue disposal to leave $450 contribution. Failed testing or unpriced disposal can remove that margin quickly. Use a licensed dismantler where the activity requires one, check fluid and battery handling obligations, and prohibit harvesting restricted equipment without documented authority. The fallback is an inspected wholesale or recycling outlet with a written acceptance specification, not an assumed scrap price.

Deadline-driven clearance turns aging inventory into a predetermined decision rather than a hopeful listing. If a machine carrying $2,400 of invested cost receives a $2,500 net wholesale offer, accepting produces $100 contribution and releases cash. Waiting three months for a projected $3,000 net realization adds $360 storage at $120 monthly and an illustrative $200 deterioration allowance, leaving only $40 contribution before other overhead. A higher selling price can therefore deliver a worse result. Set a review at day 30, a price reset at day 45, and a wholesale decision at day 60, adjusted to the category's actual sales cycle. The sixth play, section_321_de_minimis_bonded_tariff_arbitrage, belongs in a separate research ledger because it is a service model, not ordinary surplus resale. Historical arithmetic of $100,000 customs value at an assumed 25% duty yields $25,000 nominal duty; charging 40% of genuinely avoided duty would yield $10,000 service revenue before costs. Neither $100,000 customer merchandise nor $25,000 customer savings is operator revenue. This calculation establishes a measurement convention only. Do not book the fee, reserve warehouse capacity, or promise a duty-free result before verifying the current entry regime.

sections.heading: 4. Prove eligibility, custody, and cash before launch
paragraphs: The cross-border premise needs a concrete correction before any capital allocation. Executive Order 14324 directed worldwide suspension of duty-free de minimis treatment effective August 29, 2025; do not treat the historical $800 threshold or Entry Type 86 as a present entitlement. Verify subsequent changes through current CBP instructions and a licensed customs broker. Routing through Tijuana under IMMEX or a Canadian bonded warehouse does not by itself change origin, erase U.S. duties, or authorize artificial splitting of shipments. IMMEX permissions and Canadian warehouse privileges impose their own conditions and are not interchangeable with U.S. entry eligibility. The suggested Vietnam, India, EU, Bangladesh, or Cambodia fallback cannot be described as universally exempt merely because goods avoid a particular Section 301 measure. Ordinary duties and other applicable measures still require classification and origin analysis. First-sale valuation, when supported by a bona fide earlier sale for export and complete valuation evidence, can affect the dutiable value under 19 U.S.C. § 1401a; it does not eliminate the duty rate. Keep this branch unfunded until a broker validates a lawful, costed service design. Prefer domestic surplus turnover when the documentation burden exceeds the prospective service contribution.

Set up the entity, tax records, and bank accounts before registration creates binding purchase obligations. Obtain the EIN directly through the IRS where applicable, align the legal buyer name across auction accounts and payment instructions, and maintain any required state seller permits or resale certificates. An EIN is not a resale authorization, and resale treatment depends on the jurisdiction and transaction. Confirm who may bid, who may release payments, and who may collect property. Auction eligibility can vary by program, asset, and purchaser location; a public auction login does not establish eligibility for every lot. For federal personal property, review the sale framework in 41 CFR Part 102-38 together with the actual contract. Save condition representations, inspection limits, payment deadlines, removal terms, and default remedies. For defense-related assets, distinguish auction eligibility, DEMIL requirements, end-use conditions, and export controls; a DEMIL code is not an export license. Identify the relevant disposition program and required destruction or mutilation evidence before buying. Decline restricted categories that exceed the team's competence. For ordinary municipal equipment, retain a bill of sale and serial-number trail even when no vehicle title exists.

Run a simulated first lot from discovery through cash settlement before spending real inventory money. Give the worksheet to someone other than its author and ask them to reproduce the maximum bid from archived fees, tax treatment, transport quotes, repair estimates, and buyer evidence. Then rehearse the actual removal: seller contact, release document, driver identity, loading arrangement, vehicle capacity, appointment time, and backup carrier. A paid invoice without collection authority can strand a truck at the yard. Verify that storage coverage begins when risk transfers under the sale contract, not merely when the truck reaches your premises. Test the inventory record, photographic evidence, listing template, invoice, and bank reconciliation using the same lot identifier. Have a qualified technician define the minimum sale-ready tests and disclose observed defects precisely. Before launch, require four signed checks: cash survives the downside case; buyer and asset eligibility are documented; removal and custody are executable; and resale economics survive a realistic liquidation price. A failed check stops that purchase, not the entire business. chapters.question_prompt: What kills 80% of newcomers in government surplus auctions, and what forensic metrics detect margin leaks, regulatory landmines, or platform bans before they wipe out capital?
chapters.title: Beginner Traps, Clawbacks & Asymmetric Failure Modes
chapters.subtitle: GSA, GovPlanet, GovDeals and PublicSurplus: SF-97 Title Friction, DEMIL Restrictions, Removal Defaults and Lot-Level Cash Circuit-Breakers
chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, ranks #29 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score because physical execution dominates auction discovery. Annual owner net profit is $12,000 Conservative, $80,500 Base, and $200,000 Scaled, measured against gross resale proceeds rather than purchase budgets. This chapter maps six operating plays: landed-cost bid ceilings, removal-slot reservation, title-first remarketing, restricted-property segregation, aging-led liquidation, and authorized-distributor grey-market diversion arbitrage. The first five are chapter-local operating labels; the sixth is the supplied cross-market play. Each receives unit economics and a fallback. The question's 80% figure is a framing device, not an evidenced failure rate. The practical objective is to detect defects, fee leakage, title blocks, payment reversals, and account misconduct before one bad lot consumes the year's profit.

sections.heading: 1. Price the loading dock, the defect and the deadline before the hammer
paragraphs: The first fatal trap is treating an auction photograph as an inspection report; the second is treating the hammer price as inventory cost. GSA Auctions, GovPlanet, GovDeals, and PublicSurplus connect buyers with different sellers and sale conditions, not one uniform warranty regime. Download the listing, incorporated terms, amendments, photographs, payment instructions, and pickup rules before bidding. Record who owns the asset, who invoices it, and who can authorize release. An engine described as starting does not establish transmission condition, emissions readiness, diagnostic-code history, or roadworthiness. A pallet count does not establish usable-unit count. Ask for serial plates, hour meters, battery condition, missing attachments, and access dimensions; price unanswered questions as exposure rather than assuming favorable facts. Twelve usable units out of twenty nominal units turn a $2,000 purchase from $100 into $166.67 per usable unit before transport. If the seller cannot support the quantity assumption, bid on verified recoverable units or skip the lot. Keep inspection notes separate from seller representations so a later dispute identifies an actual description mismatch instead of buyer disappointment. These records also prevent the remarketing team from repeating unsupported claims to its buyers.

The landed-cost bid ceilings play starts with a defensible exit price, not the apparent discount from an obsolete catalog. For an illustrative $10,000 resale, reserve $1,200 for transport, $800 for repairs, $300 for selling costs, $500 for uncertainty, and $2,000 for contribution before shared overhead. That leaves $5,200 for hammer plus premium. With an illustrative 10% buyer premium and no acquisition tax due under a valid resale treatment, the maximum hammer is $4,727.27. If an illustrative 8% tax applies to hammer plus premium, the ceiling becomes $4,377.10. Actual taxability, premium rates, and taxable bases come from the jurisdiction and sale terms. Never substitute these example rates for the invoice. The third trap is capitalizing every optimistic repair assumption; the fourth is omitting buyer premiums, card surcharges, loading charges, or tax from the worksheet. Use auction alerts to discover inventory, but require a locked bid-limit worksheet for execution. A substitute exit at $7,500 must trigger a new ceiling, not a persuasive story. The fallback is a lower bid or no bid, preserving cash for a lot with observable demand.

Removal-slot reservation is the second play because a winning bid can create an immediate logistics liability. A municipality may require pickup during narrow staffed hours, prohibit seller loading assistance, and impose default consequences after a fixed deadline. Obtain the actual terms; there is no universal grace period. Suppose a machine can sell for $8,000 against $5,000 of acquisition and preparation costs. The expected $3,000 contribution falls to $1,000 after an $800 failed truck visit and $1,200 of additional rigging. That one dispatch error consumes one-sixth of Conservative annual owner profit. Reserve the carrier, identify forklift or crane responsibility, confirm dock geometry, and request a written release contact before bidding. Require a carrier certificate of insurance and confirm relevant cargo coverage rather than equating a certificate with coverage for every loss. Traps five through seven are assuming the seller supplies loading, assuming a dead vehicle can roll, and assuming the driver can resolve missing paperwork. The fallback is a prequoted alternate hauler within the removal window. If neither carrier can execute, do not bid; after purchase, seek a written extension immediately without treating silence as permission.

callout.title: Buy the release path before buying the apparent bargain
callout.body: Experienced buyers make the seller's physical release conditions and the downstream buyer's acceptance conditions meet before bidding.
items: Ask the property custodian for a current serial-plate photograph and a photograph of the actual loading approach; listing images may omit both.
Have the carrier quote the exact lot, dimensions, loading responsibility, and appointment window rather than a generic origin-to-destination route.

sections.heading: 2. Separate ownership, eligibility and resale rights before promising delivery
paragraphs: Title-first remarketing is the third play: ownership paperwork must support the use promised to the next buyer. An SF-97 is a federal certificate used to obtain a vehicle title, not itself a state-issued title or assurance that every state will register the vehicle for highway use. Compare the VIN on the chassis, listing, invoice, release, and certificate; identify any off-road, salvage, export-only, or destruction limitation. Check the receiving state's actual documentary and inspection requirements before advertising road-ready inventory. An illustrative $15,000 vehicle with $11,500 landed cost and $500 selling expense yields $3,000 before shared overhead. A 60-day title delay at $20 daily storage removes $1,200, even before additional capital costs. The fallback is a lawful, fully disclosed alternative buyer or parts disposition where permitted, not relabeling the vehicle or promising paperwork later. Reject unexplained serial alterations and inconsistent seller identities. UCC section 2-312 addresses title warranties in applicable commercial transactions, but the auction contract and governing law determine the actual allocation of risk. Have the documents reviewed when a defect threatens ownership, rather than assuming an as-is clause answers every title question.

Restricted-property segregation is the fourth play. GovPlanet branding, a government seller, or public visibility does not establish unrestricted civilian resale rights. Examine each lot's DEMIL designation, end-use conditions, buyer qualifications, and required certifications. A DEMIL code is not an export classification; neither automatically answers whether the Export Administration Regulations or International Traffic in Arms Regulations apply. Classify the actual article and proposed transaction, including destination, end user, and end use, before arranging export or release to a foreign buyer. An illustrative $4,000 acquisition plus $800 transport, $600 required processing, and $200 selling expense against $6,000 resale leaves only $400 before overhead. An additional $700 specialist requirement makes that route uneconomic. The fallback is an eligible domestic buyer, an authorized processing route, or declining purchase; never assume a fallback is permitted without reading the restrictions. Medical devices, communications equipment, batteries, and data-bearing computers create different controls. Keep quarantined inventory out of ordinary listings until the relevant restriction is resolved. A sales employee must not convert an unresolved classification into a shipping promise simply because a buyer offers immediate payment.

The sixth mapped play, authorized_distributor_grey_market_diversion_arbitrage, requires a tighter boundary than ordinary surplus resale. Its proposed 35–60% regional manufacturer price spread is a sourcing hypothesis, not verified margin or permission to import. Foreign purchasing entities and over-quota distributors must disclose accurate identities and transact within applicable restrictions; corporate layering does not cure missing rights. Kirtsaeng v. John Wiley & Sons concerns copyright first sale for lawfully made copies, not blanket clearance of trademarks, medical products, customs restrictions, or distributor contracts. For 100 authentic units purchased at $40 each, add $6 freight and duty, $4 inspection and labeling, and $3 selling expense per unit. Resale at $65 produces $6,500 gross proceeds and $1,200 contribution before shared overhead. A $15-per-unit return loss on twenty units reduces contribution by $300. Validate the complete return exposure separately. The preferred fallback is globally identical universal-packaging SKUs sold through documented direct B2B purchase orders, not dependence on one Amazon account. Universal packaging alone does not resolve warranty or material differences. TJX, Costco, and Burlington are potential counterparties, not assumed buyers. Exclude test strips or other regulated consumables when expiry, storage history, importer obligations, or labeling cannot be established.

callout.title: Four pre-flight checks before capital becomes trapped inventory
callout.body: A failed check stops commitment to the affected lot. It does not authorize changing documents, concealing the buyer, or substituting assumptions.
items: Verify buyer eligibility, accurate account ownership, and every lot-specific certification before entering a binding bid.
Match physical identifiers to the ownership documents and confirm the intended downstream title or transfer route.
Confirm the all-in bid ceiling, taxable case, removal funding, and downside resale route fit available unrestricted cash.

sections.heading: 3. Reconcile gross proceeds to owner profit and watch the cash tail
paragraphs: The canonical scorecard recognizes gross resale proceeds: $150,000 Conservative, $575,000 Base, and $1,000,000 Scaled. Applying 8%, 14.0%, and 20% net margins produces exactly $12,000, $80,500, and $200,000 annual owner net profit. Corresponding total annual cost envelopes are $138,000, $494,500, and $800,000. Purchases, premiums, transport, refurbishment, selling expense, and operating costs must fit inside those envelopes; do not subtract acquisition cost twice or describe auction purchases as revenue. Staffing remains 2 FT + 3 C in Conservative and Base, and 3 FT + 4 C in Scaled. These staffing counts do not establish wage rates or hours. Build an actual compensation schedule and reject any local operating plan whose costs exceed the applicable envelope. At $575,000 gross proceeds, one percentage point of margin equals $5,750 of annual profit. A $10,000 unrecovered loss consumes 12.42% of Base owner profit and 83.33% of Conservative owner profit. The stated $3,000–$15,000 monthly operating range annualizes to $36,000–$180,000, so its upper end cannot coexist with the Conservative envelope. Startup capital of $15,000–$80,000 is funding capacity, not recognized sales or an additional profit line.

Aging-led liquidation is the fifth play and the antidote to confusing listed inventory with working capital. For an illustrative $10,000 resale target against $7,500 landed inventory cost and $500 selling expense, the expected contribution is $2,000. Waiting three months at $250 monthly holding cost leaves $1,250 before shared overhead. A $9,000 immediate sale with the same selling expense leaves $1,000 and releases cash earlier; whether waiting is better depends on credible buyer demand and the next use of cash. The fallback is a prearranged regional wholesaler, parts buyer, or documented auction liquidation route with a calculated net recovery. Set internal review points at 30, 60, and 90 days from receipt, not from the date somebody finally publishes the listing. At 30 days verify inquiry quality and comparable transactions; at 60 days reprice against an executable wholesale bid; at 90 days require a written retain-or-liquidate decision. These are operator policies, not platform deadlines. Inventory tracking should expose unlisted days, blocked-title days, repair-wait days, and buyer-payment days separately. Otherwise a respectable average inventory age can conceal one expensive lot that has never become legally or physically saleable.

Build forensic telemetry around lot identifiers rather than bank balance alone. Link each invoice, carrier bill, repair order, title document, listing, buyer acceptance, and refund to the same identifier in Airtable or a controlled spreadsheet. Separate estimate revisions from actual posted costs so the team cannot erase evidence of poor bidding by overwriting the original worksheet. Review landed-cost variance weekly: a 10% overrun on a $7,500 estimate adds $750 and removes 37.5% of the illustrative $2,000 contribution. Flag a projected contribution shortfall above 25%, any missed mandatory pickup milestone, and any unresolved ownership mismatch immediately. For a new operator, limit one lot's uncommitted cash exposure to an illustrative 15% of available purchasing cash; with $50,000 available, that means $7,500 before offsetting only reliable, collectible commitments. This is a proposed circuit-breaker, not a universal safe concentration. Review weekly batches of similar lots before interpreting defect percentages from tiny samples. Two damaged units among four inspections demand investigation, not a precise population forecast. Stop new bids in the affected asset class when repeated adverse results invalidate the pricing assumptions, while continuing lawful fulfillment of existing obligations.

sections.heading: 4. Contain reversals, preserve evidence and keep platform access clean
paragraphs: Clawback is an operating shorthand, not a single government remedy. Separate an auction cancellation or rescission under governing terms from buyer default damages, downstream refunds, payment disputes, tax assessments, and recovery of improperly transferred property. Each has a different trigger, claimant, evidence trail, and recovery path. Read seller withdrawal rights and description-dispute procedures before funding repairs or promising delivery. Do not assume labor and freight become reimbursable merely because purchase money is returned. If a $6,000 acquisition is refunded after $900 freight and $600 repairs, unrecovered cash expense remains $1,500 unless those costs are separately recovered. For downstream card sales, retain the accepted description, serial numbers, delivery evidence, and correspondence, while recognizing that a signature alone does not defeat every dispute. B2B wire payment reduces some card dispute exposure but does not eliminate fraud, restitution claims, or contractual liability. Verify changes to payment instructions through a previously established contact method. When a reversal arrives, reconcile cash recovered, goods recovered, and costs still owed separately. Calling the transaction canceled must not erase an outstanding carrier bill or a buyer's property interest.

The shortcuts most likely to destroy platform access are procedural dishonesty rather than clever bidding. Shill bidding, coordinated bid suppression, account sharing contrary to platform rules, restriction evasion through replacement identities, fabricated resale certificates, and false end-use statements can produce suspension, permanent exclusion, contractual claims, or legal exposure. Do not teach a purchasing assistant to solve a suspension with another entity's account. Use named users where supported, protect credentials, and keep accurate business ownership and payment records. Bid coordination with competitors can implicate Sherman Act section 1; arranging legitimate transport capacity does not authorize discussing who will win or suppress bids. Automation should remain within permitted alerts, inventory updates, and human-reviewed bid ceilings. Unauthorized scraping or automated bidding can also breach platform terms, which must be checked directly. A municipal employee's informal suggestion does not override published eligibility restrictions or public-sale procedures. If the platform questions activity, preserve logs, pause the disputed behavior, and respond through its documented review channel. The fallback is operating only through accounts and channels where participation remains authorized, not moving the same deception somewhere harder to see.

Run incident containment as a four-step operating routine: freeze new exposure, preserve evidence, calculate recovery paths, and authorize a documented resolution. Start with the affected lot, not an indiscriminate shutdown that creates fresh pickup defaults elsewhere. Within the same business day, assign an owner, capture the exact contractual deadline, isolate questionable goods, and notify any buyer whose promised delivery or description has materially changed. Compare at least two lawful recovery routes using incremental cash, elapsed time, and enforceable conditions. Spending another $800 to obtain $500 additional recovery is a $300 deterioration, regardless of the original hammer price. Escalate suspected theft, restricted transfers, or document fabrication to qualified counsel and the appropriate counterparty without altering records. After resolution, distinguish bad luck from a repeatable process failure: missing inspection, incorrect premium formula, unreserved loading equipment, or unsupported title assumption. Update the relevant worksheet and supplier notes, then require evidence that the failed control now works before resuming comparable bids. Maintain a weekly owner review of exception exposure in dollars. A count of three incidents is less informative than knowing that one unresolved vehicle threatens half the year's expected owner profit.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, ranks #29 with a Money-to-Manpower Score of 79/100. This high-leverage, system-disciplined model rewards documented buyer demand, not optimistic bidding. Six mapped sourcing plays structure this chapter: fleet replacement resale, municipal shop-equipment resale, public-facility closure splits, inspected generator resale, restricted-screened federal equipment remarketing, and Certificate-of-Need (CON) & Decommissioned Hospital Imaging-Suite Arbitrage. Build a public-record trigger queue, qualify assets against buyer specifications, and close three to ten paid resales within a planned one-to-six-month launch window. Canonical annual owner profit is $12,000 Conservative, $80,500 Base, and $200,000 Scaled. These cases recognize gross resale proceeds, with purchase, transport, refurbishment and operating costs absorbed before owner profit.

sections.heading: 1. Mine disposal triggers before auction alerts become crowded
paragraphs: Start with one asset family and a hauling radius, not a national feed of bargains. For the first month, assign an operator to municipal fleet replacement and another to shop equipment within 200 miles; use qualified contractors for inspection, transport and repair. Build saved searches on GSA Auctions, GovDeals, PublicSurplus and GovPlanet, but record the actual seller, contract terms and asset location separately. A marketplace name does not establish federal ownership, eligibility or identical purchase conditions. Capture auction identifier, serial number, closing time, buyer premium, payment deadline, removal deadline, loading assistance and inspection access in Airtable or a spreadsheet. Apply alerts to spelling variants, model families and broad categories; a poorly labeled listing can hide an asset, but poor disclosure also hides defects. Review the queue twice daily and assign every promising lot a next action within one business day. Under 41 CFR Part 102-38, federal personal-property sales operate within a defined disposal framework; municipal terms follow the selling jurisdiction and its contract. Preserve dated terms before bidding because the operational constraint is often a two-day removal window rather than the advertised asset price. Reject listings whose access rules make a competent inspection impossible.

Work backward from public operating changes. City council agendas, capital-improvement budgets, fleet replacement schedules, school board minutes, hospital district meetings and facility-closure notices reveal likely supply before a polished listing appears. A replacement appropriation is a research trigger, not evidence that an identified vehicle will be sold. Match the approved purchase with department inventory records, a disposal resolution and the auction calendar. Send narrow public-record requests for existing disposition schedules or equipment lists; specify department, date range and preferred electronic format. Federal requests fall under 5 U.S.C. 552, while local requests use the relevant state records statute. Neither route requires an agency to create your market analysis or disclose exempt material. Ask the published surplus contact how inspection and bidding work, never for preferential award treatment. In parallel, mine demand from municipal maintenance contractors, independent repair shops, regional equipment dealers and installation firms that publish completed projects. An awarded service contract can suggest equipment demand, but confirm specifications and timing directly. Score a signal higher only when supply timing, lawful access and a named buyer need converge. Archive the source URL and publication date so another operator can reproduce the reasoning without relying on a private conversation.

Use six chapter-level sourcing plays, with the medical-imaging route mapped explicitly to con_decommissioned_medical_imaging_arbitrage. The other five routes are fleet replacement resale, municipal shop-equipment resale, public-facility closure splits, inspected generator resale and restricted-screened federal equipment remarketing. Each starts with a different buyer objection: title, calibration, handling, load performance or transfer restrictions. The matrix gives illustrative dollars per completed resale, not additional scorecard scenarios. Calculate contribution as resale receipts less landed acquisition, direct selling costs and an explicit defect reserve; contribution still must cover allocated overhead. For example, $16,000 of fleet receipts less $12,000 of direct costs produces $4,000 contribution, not $4,000 owner profit. Require a written buyer specification and two independent demand checks before underwriting a new category. For imaging, those checks must involve technically qualified purchasers rather than general equipment brokers. Price recoverable equipment independently of any operating-site authority. The fallback must exist before bidding: a documented dealer offer, feasible parts recovery where permitted, or a decision not to acquire. A reserve-price reduction does not repair missing documents or create a buyer. Revisit these routes weekly and stop sourcing categories whose inspection burden consistently consumes their apparent spread.

callout.title: Find the spread in documents, access and buyer specificity
callout.body: Experienced surplus operators investigate the friction other bidders ignore, then reject friction that cannot be priced or resolved.

sections.heading: 2. Qualify demand and cap bids before capital becomes trapped
paragraphs: Build the buyer specification before the bid worksheet. Interview prospects about required model, minimum capacity, acceptable condition, installation geography, purchasing authority and delivery deadline. Ask what would cause rejection after arrival and who can accept the asset. A buyer saying that used generators sell well is market commentary; a buyer requesting a tested 480-volt three-phase unit within thirty days is a qualified demand signal. Record the difference. Use a 100-point scorecard: twenty points each for specific buyer demand, inspected condition and verified economics; fifteen each for removal feasibility and documentation; ten for cash-cycle fit. Award full points only against evidence, half points for a documented but incomplete answer, and zero for an unanswered question. Advance at eighty points only if title, eligibility, restriction and removal checks also pass. A high score cannot offset a prohibited transfer or an impossible loading plan. Classify an unsigned price indication below an executed purchase commitment, and record any cancellation right. Require a second buyer for specialized inventory because the first buyer can change projects while the auction payment deadline remains fixed. Review every score with the person responsible for collecting payment rather than letting the sourcing operator grade their own enthusiasm.

Translate buyer evidence into a maximum hammer bid using actual auction charges. Assume a documented $20,000 resale, $1,500 transport, $1,000 refurbishment, $500 selling expense, $1,000 defect reserve, $1,500 allocated overhead and $3,000 target owner profit. These leave $11,500 for hammer price plus a ten-percent buyer premium; $11,500 divided by 1.10 yields $10,454.54 after rounding down to cents. Set the operational limit at $10,450 or lower, subject to permitted bid increments. This illustration assumes documented acquisition-tax treatment and no additional auction charge. If tax applies, calculate its actual taxable base and reduce the bid; never presume a resale certificate covers every fee or purchase. Include storage, loading, payment charges and title expenses when applicable. Treat sales tax collected for remittance separately from recognized resale revenue. Use a downside case with lower receipts and a longer holding period before approving the worksheet internally. Keep the live bid limit visible beside the lot number, and prohibit escalation because another bidder appears confident. If the next permissible bid exceeds the limit, lose the auction. The resulting purchase price determines whether good sourcing produces an actual margin.

Apply a separate diligence track to Certificate-of-Need (CON) & Decommissioned Hospital Imaging-Suite Arbitrage, the TRACK_1 play con_decommissioned_medical_imaging_arbitrage. An approved location may have strategic value to an eligible operator, but a scanner purchase does not carry the site's authority automatically. State programs differ by provider, service, project and transaction structure; New York Public Health Law section 2802 illustrates approval requirements for covered hospital projects. Obtain transaction-specific review before assigning value to continued operations or a change in control. Illustratively, $60,000 equipment receipts minus $25,000 acquisition, $8,000 qualified deinstallation, $4,000 transport, $5,000 technical testing and $3,000 reserve produce $15,000 contribution before overhead. Budget an MRI separately for magnet management, cryogens and specialized rigging; do not reuse a CT removal estimate. Confirm software rights, service access, data sanitization and required radiation-equipment obligations for the equipment involved. FDA rules in 21 CFR 1020.30 address diagnostic X-ray systems, not every imaging modality. A negotiated option may make specified approvals a closing condition; a binding auction purchase usually offers no invented exit right. If authority cannot transfer as contemplated, exercise an actual contractual contingency or sell inspected equipment separately without representing transferable operating authority.

sections.heading: 3. Turn buyer intent into replies, inspections and enforceable sales
paragraphs: Run a buyer-first cadence against a small, researched account list. Select thirty regional businesses whose published work matches your chosen asset family, identify the purchasing role, and use publicly listed business contact channels. On day one, send a brief email naming the relevant specification and asking whether the business buys that equipment used. On day three, make one manual business call to confirm the appropriate contact. On day six, send a one-page specification sheet with inspection status, expected timing and a clearly labeled indicative price. On day ten, close the loop with a direct question about fit and stop if they decline. For an unowned auction asset, state that acquisition is pending; do not imply possession or guaranteed delivery. Commercial email must satisfy 15 U.S.C. 7704, including accurate headers, required identification, a valid postal address and a working opt-out process. Honor opt-outs within the statutory period and suppress them across your list. Avoid automated texts and prerecorded outreach; 47 U.S.C. 227 and implementing rules create additional requirements. Track the last touch, reply substance and next step, not merely email opens. Platform listings and trade-directory inquiries should feed the same evidence trail.

Use inbound content to answer purchase objections rather than collect anonymous traffic. Publish one category page containing supported makes, normal inspection scope, service radius and a form requesting model, budget, deadline and installation location. For owned inventory, publish original photographs, serial details appropriate for public disclosure, measured dimensions and known defects. Offer the complete inspection packet through a controlled link; remove personal records and seller information that you lack permission to redistribute. A regional equipment dealer, rigging company or independent service technician can introduce qualified buyers, but document any referral fee and avoid arrangements with public employees that could distort disposal decisions. Price freight as a distinct quoted component so a buyer can compare delivered and collected terms. When a prospect says the asset is too expensive, ask whether the comparison includes testing, loading and delivery; then show the specific difference without inventing competitor defects. When they require a warranty you cannot support, refer them to a service provider or decline the promise. When they need equipment immediately, offer only inventory whose release and transport timing are confirmed. Good objection handling narrows the transaction to facts both parties can accept instead of widening your liability.

Measure conversion by cohort and keep demand activity separate from recognized sales. An illustrative launch target is 120 researched accounts producing 60 verified contacts, 24 substantive replies, 12 qualified requirements, six written conditional purchase commitments and three completed, paid resales. The successive conversion targets are 50%, 40%, 50%, 50% and 50%; overall paid conversion is 2.5%. These are planning hypotheses, not observed industry rates. A conditional commitment is useful evidence but does not make an auction acquisition riskless. Define price, serial identity where available, condition, inspection rights, delivery responsibility and the consequence of failing to acquire the asset. Record deposits as liabilities until the applicable revenue-recognition conditions are met; never count a signed mandate or refundable deposit as gross resale proceeds. Track days from first contact to specification, specification to commitment and acquisition to collected resale. If replies are weak, revise targeting and relevance before buying more leads. If qualified requirements fail to convert, inspect pricing, condition evidence and delivery risk. If commitments fail after acquisition, investigate cancellation terms and acceptance disputes. Diagnose each bottleneck separately so outreach volume cannot conceal an inventory problem or justify speculative purchasing.

sections.heading: 4. Execute the first three-to-ten wins and reconcile the actual margin
paragraphs: Stage the first one-to-six-month campaign around evidence milestones. During weeks one and two, select the category, contact thirty buyers, identify ten recurring sellers and obtain inspection and hauling quotes. During weeks three through six, complete the qualification worksheets, inspect suitable lots and pursue one manageable acquisition whose payment and removal obligations fit available cash. During weeks seven through twelve, deliver the first paid resales and use acceptance results to improve the specification sheet. During months four through six, repeat only the combinations of seller, asset and buyer that produced positive realized contribution. Count a win as a completed sale with collected payment and documented delivery acceptance, not an auction victory. Three wins might establish a workable route; ten should demonstrate repeatability across more than one purchaser. Do not multiply the funnel mechanically to force ten transactions when inventory turns slowly. With startup capital of $15,000–$80,000 and monthly operating expense of $3,000–$15,000, the low end cannot support several specialized lots plus months of storage. Maintain a rolling thirteen-week cash forecast and reserve funds for removal, defects and operating bills before allocating another bid budget. Separate owner distributions from available buying cash.

Treat transfer and release documents as inventory attributes. For applicable federal vehicle sales, Standard Form 97 supports an application for state title; it is not itself a state-issued title or proof that every registration requirement has been satisfied. Confirm the destination state's process before promising a road-ready vehicle. For defense-origin equipment, review the listing's demilitarization designation, end-use documentation and release requirements with the seller. A DEMIL code is not a universal resale license. The U.S. Munitions List in 22 CFR 121.1 and controls under the Export Administration Regulations require transaction-specific classification and screening when applicable; domestic acquisition does not establish unrestricted export rights. At pickup, match serials, count accessories, photograph condition and obtain a signed release before loading. Follow sale terms for discrepancies rather than assuming returns are available. On resale, use a written agreement addressing condition, inspection, payment, risk transfer and delivery acceptance under the applicable state's enacted UCC rules. Keep inspection claims consistent with what was actually tested. Route imaging data sanitization through authorized personnel and retain a certificate identifying the handled equipment, without copying patient information into your deal file. Close the record only after funds settle and obligations are documented.

Reconcile completed transactions to the canonical annual scorecard without converting contribution into owner profit. Conservative revenue is $150,000 at 8%, yielding $12,000 owner net profit and $138,000 total annual costs with 2 FT + 3 C. Base revenue is $575,000 at 14.0%, yielding $80,500 owner net profit and $494,500 costs with 2 FT + 3 C. Scaled revenue is $1,000,000 at 20%, yielding $200,000 owner net profit and $800,000 costs with 3 FT + 4 C. These totals include acquisition, transport, refurbishment and operating expenses; do not deduct them twice. Team labels do not establish affordable compensation, so test actual hours and local rates within each cost envelope. Ten illustrative $16,000 fleet resales produce $160,000 receipts and, at $12,000 direct cost each, $40,000 contribution before overhead; they do not equal the Conservative case. Never include a customer's hauling revenue or hospital service receipts as operator resale revenue. Review contribution by lot, holding days, forecast error and buyer concentration each month. Use a prewritten aging policy to seek fresh dealer bids and reduce price when carrying costs exceed a defensible recovery upside. Reorder evidence-backed inventory, not merely categories that generated entertaining auctions.

chapters.pull_quote: The best surplus deal is the asset whose buyer, removal plan and downside exit are documented before the first bid.
action_checklist: Choose one asset family and a 200-mile initial hauling radius; configure seller-specific alerts across the relevant auction platforms.
Build a thirty-account buyer list and capture model, capacity, condition, budget, delivery date and purchasing authority for each qualified requirement.
Connect disposal resolutions and replacement budgets to actual listings; retain dated public records without treating planned disposal as confirmed availability.
Complete inspection, transfer, restriction and removal checks, then calculate a bid ceiling including fees, taxes, reserves and allocated overhead.
Run the ten-day email, manual-call and specification cadence; track conversion from researched account through collected resale rather than signed interest alone.
Close three paid sales before expanding categories, then reconcile each lot and the annual forecast against the exact Conservative, Base and Scaled scorecard.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, holds Rank #29 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score because physical custody, working capital and exception handling dominate execution. This chapter maps six operator plays: discover and score; verify and bid; fund and remove; triage and refurbish; remarket to businesses; reconcile and recycle capital. A two full-time, three-contractor pod runs those plays through evidence-linked lot records, serialized SQLite transactions and immutable journals. The worked quarter produces $143,750 gross resale revenue and $20,125 owner profit, annualizing to the $80,500 Base case. Conservative annual owner profit remains $12,000; Scaled remains $200,000. The operating test is whether title, custody, inventory cost, receivables and bank cash reconcile without treating unsold assets as earnings.

sections.heading: 1. Assign six plays to one five-person pod before bidding
paragraphs: Start with one narrow asset lane: ordinary commercial shop equipment with identifiable models, accessible loading and reachable business buyers. The six plays here are the chapter's operational mapping of Candidate #17, not six independent businesses. Full-time operator A owns discovery, bid limits and buyer relationships; full-time operator B owns verification, custody records and the ledger. Three contractors provide scheduled hauling, mechanical inspection and bookkeeping review. Contractor availability is purchased by job, not assumed to equal three additional salaried positions. Use GSA Auctions for applicable federal sales, GovDeals and PublicSurplus for participating public sellers, and GovPlanet only after identifying the actual seller and applicable lot terms. Marketplace branding does not establish federal ownership, transferable title or unrestricted resale. Each morning, operator A imports permitted alerts and records the source URL, seller, auction identifier, closing time, location, asset description and inspection window. Operator B rejects missing ownership evidence or impossible removal logistics before anyone spends inspection money. Keep an immutable copy of the listing and amendments; a changed pickup term can destroy the economics of an otherwise attractive machine. Assign each lot one accountable owner and one next action with a timestamp.

Convert discovery into a maximum all-in commitment, not an emotional hammer-price target. Establish a defensible resale estimate from completed transactions, dealer quotations and named buyer conversations, then subtract selling fees, transport, repair allowance, required contribution and carrying cost. If expected resale is $10,000, selling costs are $600, transport $800, repairs $900 and required contribution $2,000, only $5,700 remains for hammer price, premium and nonrecoverable acquisition taxes combined. At a hypothetical ten percent premium with no acquisition tax, the hammer ceiling is $5,181.81, rounded downward to the permitted increment. Actual premium and tax treatment come from that sale's terms. Do not substitute a resale permit for evidence that the seller accepts it. Score removal feasibility separately from price: a cheap lathe requiring an unavailable rigger is not an executable purchase. Inspection records must distinguish observed operation, seller statements and untested functions. Photograph serial plates, power requirements and missing attachments; ask whether loading assistance is contractual or merely customary. Auction alerts and bid worksheets automate sorting, while operator A retains responsibility for the submitted bid and available cash reservation.

Verification must resolve sale eligibility, restrictions and ownership before a funded award enters the removal queue. For federal property, read the sale-specific terms alongside 41 CFR Part 102-38; municipal sales follow their own authority and contract conditions rather than automatically inheriting federal procedures. A vehicle's SF-97 supports an application for a state title; it is not itself a universally usable state title or permission to operate the vehicle. Confirm the destination state's documents, liens, identification checks and dealer-license thresholds before bidding repeatedly in vehicles. For defense-origin assets, inspect the assigned demilitarization requirements and any end-use certificate conditions. Never infer unrestricted status from photographs or a seller's casual description. Route export-sensitive goods through item-specific classification and destination review; the baseline lane excludes weapons, munitions and unresolved controlled equipment. Operator B records the evidence supporting every check, while the relevant contractor confirms practical removability. Escalation means stopping that lot, not stopping the entire business. The remaining pipeline continues through inspected, ordinary assets whose transfer and resale are documented. This separation protects the five-person pod from spending its week untangling a single restricted or undocumented purchase.

callout.title: Four tactics that protect recovery value
callout.body: The best bid advantage is often better removal and buyer evidence, not faster clicking.
items: Ask the property custodian for doorway dimensions, forklift capacity and appointment rules before hiring the hauler; retain the written response with the lot.
Photograph the serial plate during inspection and again at pickup; mixed municipal storage yards can release a visually similar but different machine.
Obtain a parts-only buyer quote before bidding on untested equipment, then use that quote as a documented downside recovery rather than a retail listing.
Schedule the inspection contractor and hauler together where practical; one coordinated site visit can expose rigging costs before an irreversible bid.

sections.heading: 2. Install a serialized ledger and evidence-bound state machine
paragraphs: Use a local SQLite ledger as the authoritative economic record, with one database on a local disk and one connection per operation. The six modules below concatenate into a runnable standard-library reference implementation. Set the database path explicitly, deploy schema changes before accepting writes, and keep application access behind an authenticated operator service. SQLite WAL improves reader concurrency; BEGIN IMMEDIATE serializes writers before they inspect inventory state. Every mutation has a unique operation key, canonical payload and atomic journal. Reusing the same key and payload returns the original result; reusing it with different content raises an error. A stale transition fails rather than silently overwriting another operator's work. Unique marketplace and source-lot identifiers prevent duplicate intake, while journal lines use integer cents and debit-positive signs. Balanced entries are checked inside the write transaction. The design eliminates check-then-write races within these application functions; it does not claim that a local database can make an external auction payment exactly once. Give only the service account database write access, preserve evidence outside the database by content hash, and test restore procedures before committing meaningful auction capital.

The workflow separates verified, awarded, funded, removed, ready, sold and closed states. Verification captures five explicit checks covering eligibility, ownership, restrictions, removal and buyer economics. Those checks summarize evidence; they do not replace the underlying records. Funding debits acquisition clearing and credits cash, then removal reclassifies that amount into inventory when the illustrative custody policy recognizes the asset. Adapt recognition timing to the actual sale contract with the bookkeeper. The clearing account is not a claim that GSA or another marketplace offers escrow. Where actual third-party escrow exists, maintain its separate confirmation and reconcile the corresponding asset balance. Repairs paid before sale increase inventory cost through an explicit operation; sale books receivables, gross resale revenue and the full recorded cost. Collection reduces receivables only after bank evidence supports the receipt. Closing requires the lot's receivable to equal zero. A full-lot disposal uses the scrap transition and expenses remaining cost, preserving the failed purchase rather than deleting it. Partial write-downs, returns, taxes collected and credit sales with complex adjustments require additional reviewed posting templates before use; they are outside this deliberately bounded whole-lot reference implementation.

External execution remains a controlled handoff. Operator A submits a bid through the authorized marketplace interface; operator B records the award only after receiving a seller-issued result. Before funding, operator B checks the invoice reference against the bank and existing payment records. If an external request times out, inspect its status instead of sending another payment. The funded transition is posted after confirmation, using the confirmation identifier as the operation key. This ordering leaves an observable recovery task if the local process crashes after payment but before recording it. A subsequent bank reconciliation supplies the missing journal without repeating the transfer. Evidence identifiers should reference append-only documents, not mutable desktop filenames. The reconciliation view exposes each lot's cost, proceeds, receivable and workflow state so the bookkeeping contractor can inspect exceptions without editing source transactions. Run the quality checks after every import and before releasing another bidding budget. Back up through SQLite's backup interface, not an uncoordinated copy of an active database file. Test identical retries, conflicting retries, stale transitions and concurrent duplicate collections in a temporary database. Never run that destructive test harness against the operating ledger.

def intake(source, source_lot, evidence, resale_cents,
           reserve_cents, premium_bps, checks):
    cents(resale_cents)
    cents(reserve_cents, True)
    if type(premium_bps) is not int or premium_bps < 0:
        raise ValueError("nonnegative premium basis points required")
    if not source or not source_lot or not evidence:
        raise ValueError("source identifiers and evidence required")
    names = ("comps", "inspection", "removal", "buyer", "documents")
    if set(checks) != set(names):
        raise ValueError("five scoring checks required")
    if any(type(checks[name]) is not bool for name in names):
        raise ValueError("scoring checks must be boolean")
    score = sum(20 for name in names if checks[name])
    budget = max(0, resale_cents - reserve_cents)
    limit = budget * 10000 // (10000 + premium_bps)
    payload = canonical({
        "source": source, "source_lot": source_lot,
        "evidence": evidence, "resale": resale_cents,
        "reserve": reserve_cents, "premium_bps": premium_bps,
        "checks": checks
    })
    with transaction() as con:
        old = con.execute(
            "SELECT id, intake_payload FROM lots "
            "WHERE source=? AND source_lot=?",
            (source, source_lot)
        ).fetchone()
        if old:
            if old["intake_payload"] != payload:
                raise ValueError("conflicting intake; review amended listing")
            return old["id"]
        cur = con.execute(
            "INSERT INTO lots(source,source_lot,intake_payload,"
            "bid_limit_cents,score) VALUES(?,?,?,?,?)",
            (source, source_lot, payload, limit, score)
        )
        return cur.lastrowid

def install_views():
    con = connect()
    try:
        con.executescript('''
CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS account_balances AS
SELECT a.name AS account, COALESCE(SUM(e.cents),0) AS cents
FROM accounts a LEFT JOIN entries e ON e.account=a.name
GROUP BY a.name;

CREATE VIEW IF NOT EXISTS lot_reconciliation AS
SELECT l.id, l.source, l.source_lot, l.state, l.cost_cents,
 COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.account='inventory'
                  THEN e.cents ELSE 0 END),0) AS inventory_cents,
 COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.account='clearing'
                  THEN e.cents ELSE 0 END),0) AS clearing_cents,
 COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.account='receivable'
                  THEN e.cents ELSE 0 END),0) AS due_cents,
 -COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.account='revenue'
                   THEN e.cents ELSE 0 END),0) AS resale_cents,
 COALESCE(SUM(CASE WHEN e.account='cogs'
                  THEN e.cents ELSE 0 END),0) AS cogs_cents
FROM lots l
LEFT JOIN operations o ON o.lot_id=l.id
LEFT JOIN entries e ON e.operation_id=o.id
GROUP BY l.id, l.source, l.source_lot, l.state, l.cost_cents;
''')
    finally:
        con.close()

def snapshot():
    con = connect()
    try:
        con.execute("BEGIN")
        accounts = [dict(row) for row in con.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM account_balances ORDER BY account"
        )]
        lots = [dict(row) for row in con.execute(
            "SELECT * FROM lot_reconciliation ORDER BY id"
        )]
        con.commit()
        return {"accounts": accounts, "lots": lots}
    finally:
        con.close()

sections.heading: 3. Walk a 90-day cohort from initial capital to Base-case cash
paragraphs: The worked cohort begins with $75,000 unrestricted owner capital, zero inventory, zero receivables and no debt. It assumes a prepared buyer network and executable auction access; it is a production illustration, not a promise that a cold start generates sales immediately. Candidate #17's stated time to first deal remains one to six months. Over the quarter, the pod screens 108 leads, rejects 42 before purchase and acquires 27 lots. Twenty-one lots sell and six remain on hand. Each month's sales cohort means lots accepted by buyers that month, including carryover purchases; it does not imply that every sale originated in the same month's lead pool. Acquisition and preparation cash totals $126,625. This includes hammer prices, premiums, nonrecoverable acquisition taxes, inbound transport and direct refurbishment. All acquired lots clear removal within their purchase month, leaving no acquisition-clearing balance at month end. Selling fees and routine outbound delivery are paid inside the stated operating expense budget. Sales tax collected for a jurisdiction would be a liability, not resale revenue; this example assumes documented business resale transactions with no sales tax collected. Opening capital is funding, never revenue or owner profit.

Month one sells five lots for $35,000 and collects $30,000, leaving $5,000 receivable. Cash acquisition and preparation payments of $45,000 exceed recognized cost of goods sold of $27,178, so inventory ends at $17,822. After $4,000 operating expense, owner profit is $3,822 while operating cash flow is negative $19,000. Month two sells seven lots for $47,500, collects $45,000, pays $40,000 into inventory and recognizes $36,886 cost of goods sold. Inventory reaches $20,936 and receivables reach $7,500; monthly profit is $6,614 but cash increases only $1,000. Month three sells nine lots for $61,250 and collects $63,750, including older invoices. It pays $41,625 for acquisitions and preparation, recognizes $47,561 cost of goods sold and spends $4,000 on operations. Profit is $9,689 and cash increases $18,125. The three cost figures include defect-related overruns of $500, $750 and $1,000 on sold lots. These are already expenses through cost of goods sold, not additional deductions. Prepurchase scrubs consume staff time covered by overhead but create no inventory asset or separate invented cash loss.

At day ninety, gross resale revenue is $143,750, cost of goods sold is $111,625 and operating expense is $12,000. Owner profit therefore equals $20,125, exactly fourteen percent of revenue. Cash ends at $75,125, inventory at $15,000 and receivables at $5,000. The balance sheet reconciles: $95,125 of assets equals $75,000 contributed capital plus $20,125 retained profit. The cash bridge is equally important: $20,125 profit minus $15,000 inventory growth minus $5,000 receivable growth equals $125 operating cash inflow. Four quarters at the same revenue and expense economics yield $575,000 gross revenue, $446,500 cost of goods sold, $48,000 operating expense and $80,500 owner profit. Do not multiply the startup quarter's inventory buildup indefinitely when estimating mature cash generation. A steady portfolio can replenish sold stock while holding working capital approximately constant. This model assumes the two full-time operators are working owners whose compensation comes from residual owner profit; the $4,000 monthly overhead includes contractor work and ordinary business expenses, not two market-rate salaries. Hiring replacement employees requires rebuilding the economics. Owner income tax, financing and distributions are outside this unlevered illustration.

sections.heading: 4. Control exceptions, prove custody and release the next bidding budget
paragraphs: Removal is the first production bottleneck because the auction clock does not pause for contractor scheduling. Immediately after award, operator B obtains the seller's release procedure, appointment contact and final removal date, then books the hauler against documented dimensions and weight. Confirm whether the site permits dismantling, requires specific insurance or prohibits seller-operated loading. The pickup packet contains paid receipt, authorization for the named driver, asset identifiers and photographs of expected attachments. At handoff, record discrepancies before departure and follow the seller's stated dispute procedure; do not assume an as-is sale includes a repair remedy. For interstate commercial hauling, verify the carrier's operating authority and insurance through official FMCSA records when applicable to the movement. The contractor's pickup signature establishes a custody event, not a conclusion about legal ownership. Receiving inspection reconciles count, serial number, visible damage and delivered accessories. Operator B then selects repair, direct resale or documented disposal. Any repair extension requires a fresh recovery comparison, including storage days and buyer demand. The physical inventory label must retain the ledger lot identifier even when equipment is moved between warehouse bays.

Remarketing begins before pickup but promises remain tied to inspected facts. Operator A builds a buyer packet with model, serial number, power requirements, observed test results, condition photographs and precise pickup or delivery responsibilities. Distinguish a powered-on test from verified performance under load. Use direct outreach to local fabricators, fleet service businesses, equipment dealers and other qualified commercial buyers before paying broad marketplace fees. A dealer liquidation quote gives the pod a concrete exit option when storage and repair begin eroding contribution. Written quotations should address inspection, acceptance, title transfer, delivery cost and payment timing. State enactments of UCC Article 2 govern many goods transactions; review the applicable provisions rather than relying on a generic auction slogan. For example, California Commercial Code section 2312 addresses title warranties, while section 2316 governs warranty exclusions within its scope. Match condition statements across the listing, invoice and delivery record so a persuasive sales description does not contradict the actual evidence. Do not advertise unrestricted exportability merely because a domestic acquisition was permitted. The commercial goal is repeatable, accurately described inventory that business buyers can evaluate without expensive follow-up surprises.

Release capital weekly using a conservative cash schedule, not the income statement alone. Operator B starts with reconciled bank cash, subtracts unpaid commitments, scheduled hauling, necessary repairs and the next overhead cycle, then offers operator A a bounded bidding allocation. Receivables become available cash only after collection; unsold inventory remains tied-up capital even when an asking price suggests a gain. Review aging by days since custody and days since first listing, because a slow repair queue and a weak buyer market require different fixes. The bookkeeping contractor checks journal balance, source documents and the inventory rollforward each month; an independent physical count challenges the ledger's existence assumptions. Keep a correction trail through reviewed reversal entries in an extended system rather than deleting posted history. The reference implementation intentionally refuses unsupported corrections until that mechanism exists. Compare realized margins with the canonical eight, fourteen and twenty percent scenarios, but do not label a temporary cash surplus as higher profitability. Scaling to $1,000,000 revenue and $200,000 owner profit requires three full-time people and four contractors in the scorecard. The five-person Base pod should improve cycle time before adding geography, restricted categories or a larger speculative stock position.

chapters.executive_summary: Candidate #17, Government Surplus Auctions, ranks #29 with a 79/100 Money-to-Manpower Score. Its information edge comes from six mapped operating plays: federal fleet resale, municipal equipment resale, commercial equipment bundling, repair-led resale, documented parts recovery, and buyer-led B2B remarketing. This chapter maps those plays to public records, authorized commercial interfaces, inspection evidence, and a compact decision pipeline. Annual owner profit remains $12,000 Conservative, $80,500 Base, and $200,000 Scaled; gross resale proceeds, rather than auction-platform transaction volume, are the revenue basis. A two-full-time, three-contractor pod should automate discovery and reconciliation while keeping title, restrictions, bid ceilings, and removal feasibility under explicit human ownership. Better data earns its keep only when it changes a purchase decision or accelerates cash recovery.

sections.heading: 1. Map eighteen sources to six repeatable buying plays
paragraphs: Define six operating plays before connecting a single source: P1 federal fleet resale, P2 municipal equipment resale, P3 commercial equipment bundling, P4 repair-led resale, P5 documented parts recovery, and P6 buyer-led B2B remarketing. These are this chapter's execution mapping for Candidate #17, not six additional revenue lines. A truck can move through P1, P4, and P6 without generating revenue three times. Give every acquired asset one inventory identity and recognize its resale proceeds once. Full-time operator A owns sourcing, inspections, and bid authorization; full-time operator B owns records, inventory, buyer development, and collections. The three contractors provide mechanical inspection, transport or rigging, and bookkeeping support through scheduled assignments rather than continuous staffing. Direct federal fleet opportunities toward VIN and title evidence; municipal machinery toward serial numbers, maintenance records, attachments, and removal conditions. Bundles need component counts, repair plays need fault isolation, parts recovery needs disposition restrictions, and buyer-led remarketing needs written specifications. This routing prevents a five-person pod from researching every listing equally. Restrict the initial territory to assets that existing carriers can remove within the posted window, then expand only after completed sales establish real handling costs and buyer demand.

Treat the directory below as an access map, not a claim that every vendor publishes an unrestricted API. GSA Auctions is a federal sales portal; GovPlanet, GovDeals, and Public Surplus are commercial marketplaces whose sellers, contract terms, and data permissions vary. A government seller does not make a platform's authenticated interface public infrastructure. Use account alerts, permitted exports, documented interfaces, and seller correspondence first. Do not reverse-engineer private endpoints or defeat access controls. The directory distinguishes free public lookup from paid reports, transaction charges, and credentialed developer access. Exact commercial prices and numeric quotas belong in the desk's dated provider register after checking current terms; invented universal figures would create bad purchasing rules. Refresh intervals below are desk schedules, not promises about source publication speed. Listings can change near closing, official records can lag, and provider reports can inherit that lag. Recheck auction amendments before bidding and preserve the seller's actual terms separately from aggregator summaries. When a source offers no supported bulk route, reduce the candidate list before manual lookup instead of building a fragile scraper. Record who retrieved each document, when it was retrieved, and which lot identifier it supports.

Apply an enrichment waterfall that spends effort only when the next answer can alter a decision. First capture lot identity, seller, location, closing time, payment terms, removal deadline, photographs, and restrictions. Second resolve manufacturer, model, serial number, VIN, quantities, and included attachments. Third obtain independent condition and ownership evidence. Fourth estimate resale demand and freight with sources appropriate to the asset. Fifth request missing records directly from the agency or seller before paying for deeper reports. Federal requests under 5 U.S.C. § 552 can target existing maintenance records, disposal descriptions, and releasable historical sale records; they do not compel an agency to create an appraisal or answer engineering questions. Municipal requests follow the relevant state records statute and custodian procedures. Specify equipment identifiers, date ranges, desired electronic format, and a fee ceiling. Request operational records rather than employee contact details. Records response time rarely fits an imminent auction close, so build recurring agency relationships and request prior-period records ahead of inventory cycles. Attach each result to its asset and retain a clear distinction between seller assertions, official records, commercial reports, and the pod's own inspection findings. Conflicting evidence should lower the bid ceiling or stop the purchase.
